title: Mean Girls
logline: A homeschooled teen navigates a high-school clique. Tina Fey script: dense, quotable one-liners and satire.
overview: Cady Heron is a hit with The Plastics, the A-list girl clique at her new school, until she makes the mistake of falling for Aaron Samuels, the ex-boyfriend of alpha Plastic Regina George.

jokes.text: Cady's mom treats her 16-year-old like a kindergartner on the first day of school — packing her lunch with a dollar for milk and writing down the phone number
jokes.setup: A parent tearfully prepares their child for the first day of school — classic emotional parental moment
jokes.punchline: Cady's voiceover reveals she is 16, not 5, making the coddling absurdly mismatched
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection that opens the film with a strong laugh. The setup is played completely straight — we hear the dialogue before we know the age — so the reveal lands cleanly. Good structure and economy; the joke does exactly what it needs to in four seconds.

jokes.text: "I know what you're thinking. Home-schooled kids are freaks." Cut to: X-Y-L-O-C-A-R-P. Xylocarp.
jokes.setup: Cady preemptively defends home-schoolers against the stereotype that they are freaks
jokes.punchline: Immediately cuts to a kid spelling an obscure word at a spelling bee, illustrating exactly the freak stereotype she's denying
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic juxtaposition. The joke is entirely structural — Cady's denial is instantly and perfectly undercut by visual evidence. Economy is near-flawless: one cut, one obscure word, joke complete. The irony is self-aware without being smug.

jokes.text: "Or that we're weirdly religious or something." Cut to: 'And on the third day, God created the Remington bolt-action rifle so that Man could fight the dinosaurs. And the homosexuals.'
jokes.setup: Cady again preemptively denies the stereotype — this time that home-schoolers are weirdly religious
jokes.punchline: Cut to a home-school lesson conflating Genesis, dinosaurs, and homophobia with a rifle — the most exaggerated possible version of the stereotype she just denied
jokes.explanation: Escalates the previous joke's formula with sharper, darker content. The specificity — bolt-action rifle, dinosaurs, homosexuals, all crammed into one sentence — is what elevates it. The 'Amen. Amen.' button is perfect. Dark subversive territory handled with confidence.

jokes.text: Cady nervously introduces herself to a student: 'Talk to me again and I'll kick your ass.'
jokes.setup: Cady, nervous and earnest, tries to make a friend on her first day
jokes.punchline: The student responds with an immediate, unprovoked threat, completely subverting the expected social norm
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean visual/dialogue gag. The brutality of the response is funny precisely because Cady's approach was so gentle. Economy is excellent — no setup bloat. Slightly generic in character terms (could be any mean student), which limits the score.

jokes.text: "He farts a lot." — a student warns Cady about sitting next to Kristen Hadley's boyfriend, then after the boyfriend sits down, the student leans over to explain
jokes.setup: A student warns Cady not to sit somewhere because someone's boyfriend will sit there — implying a social-hierarchy reason
jokes.punchline: The actual reason is simply that he farts a lot
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection into low-brow simplicity. The build-up suggests social politics; the reveal is base and blunt. It works because of the deadpan delivery timing and the utter banality of the reason. Not sophisticated but well-timed.

jokes.text: Mr. Duvall notices his T-shirt is stuck to his sweater mid-introduction to the class
jokes.setup: Mr. Duvall enters the classroom to introduce the new student — an authority figure in professional context
jokes.punchline: He's visibly disheveled, shirt stuck to sweater, undercutting his authority immediately
jokes.explanation: Light physical comedy that humanizes Duvall efficiently. Not especially original but serves character establishment. The self-aware "Fantastic" sells it.

jokes.text: Teacher's summer update: 'I got divorced. My carpal tunnel came back.' Mr. Duvall: 'I win.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Duvall casually asks a colleague how her summer was
jokes.punchline: She lists two miseries; he one-ups her with 'I win' — treating suffering as a competition with casual acceptance
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'I win' reframes adult misery as a game, which is both darkly funny and characterizes both teachers instantly. The structure is tight: two complaints, one escalation, one three-word button. This is good Tina Fey economy.

jokes.text: Mr. Duvall mispronounces 'Cady' as 'Caddy,' apologizes, then pivots to a story about his nephew Anfernee — 'almost as mad as I get when I think about the fact that my sister named him Anfernee'
jokes.setup: Mr. Duvall apologizes for mispronouncing Cady's name and draws a comparison to his nephew with an unusual name
jokes.punchline: He reveals he's actually angrier at his sister for choosing the name than his nephew is at being called the wrong thing — turning a moment of empathy into a personal grievance
jokes.explanation: One of the best Duvall jokes in the film. The pivot from professional courtesy to personal family grievance is a great character beat — it reveals his simmering frustrations beneath the administrator facade. 'Anfernee' is a genuinely funny name choice. The structure has a clean second surprise: we expect the story to be about the nephew's feelings, not his own.

jokes.text: Cady asks to use the bathroom; teacher refuses to give her the lavatory pass despite her asking politely — 'Nice try. Have a seat.'
jokes.setup: Cady, raised in a home-school environment of trust, innocently asks to use the bathroom
jokes.punchline: The teacher treats it as a manipulation attempt — 'Nice try' — illustrating the institutional suspicion Cady has never encountered
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke about institutional distrust vs. Cady's naivete. Works as character comedy and satire of school bureaucracy. 'Nice try' applied to a genuine bathroom request is the core absurdity.

jokes.text: 'Don't read ahead! No green pen! No food in class!' — a rapid-fire montage of teachers yelling arbitrary rules at Cady
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover says she got in trouble for 'the most random things'
jokes.punchline: The rules are genuinely random and petty — especially 'no green pen' — delivered as if they carry equal weight to serious infractions
jokes.explanation: The 'no green pen' specificity is what saves this from being generic. The rapid montage format is a well-worn device but executed crisply. Serves the thematic point about institutional arbitrariness.

jokes.text: 'Did you see nipple? It only counts if you saw a nipple.' 'That's true, dude.'
jokes.setup: Two boys are apparently discussing witnessing some kind of wardrobe malfunction
jokes.punchline: Their earnest debate about the technical criteria for what 'counts' treats it like a legal or sporting rule
jokes.explanation: The joke lands on the boys' pedantic seriousness — the word 'counts' frames it as a rulebook. Juxtaposed with Cady's voiceover about having friends in Africa, it's a sharp commentary on what she's walked into. Good economy.

jokes.text: Janis: 'This is Damian. He's almost too gay to function.'
jokes.setup: Janis introduces her best friend Damian to Cady
jokes.punchline: The introduction is 'he's almost too gay to function' — delivered as a matter-of-fact credential, not an insult
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The word 'almost' is doing enormous structural work — it's the precision of 'almost too gay to function' that's funny, not just the bluntness. It's Janis's specific voice, and the affectionate deadpan tone reframes what could be a slur into a loving character sketch. High originality, perfect economy, strong character integration. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: 'Nice wig, Janis. What's it made of?' 'Your mom's chest hair!'
jokes.setup: An offhand insult about Janis's wig from a passing student
jokes.punchline: Janis fires back instantly with 'your mom's chest hair' — a specific, gross, escalating comeback
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'chest hair' makes this funnier than a standard 'your mom' joke. It tells us immediately that Janis is sharp, quick, and has no patience for nonsense. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Watch out, please! New meat coming through!'
jokes.setup: Janis is guiding Cady through the crowded hallway
jokes.punchline: She announces Cady as 'new meat' — treating the school's social ecosystem like a predator-prey environment, foreshadowing the film's themes
jokes.explanation: Light but efficient. 'New meat' is thematically resonant with the zoo/Africa motif the film has established. Janis's bravado is characterful.

jokes.text: 'You're taking 12th-grade calculus?' 'Yeah, I like math.' 'Why?' 'Because it's the same in every country.' 'That's beautiful. This girl is deep.'
jokes.setup: Janis is surprised Cady takes advanced math; Cady explains her practical reason for liking it
jokes.punchline: Damian interprets a purely functional observation as profound philosophy — 'This girl is deep'
jokes.explanation: Layered joke: Cady's answer is sincere and literal, Damian's reaction is hilariously over-the-top, and Janis's silence (implied) is perfect contrast. Establishes Cady's outsider perspective while giving Damian a good character moment. The word 'deep' applied to arithmetic is the comedic incongruity that sells it.

jokes.text: 'Where's the back building?' 'It burned down in 1987.'
jokes.setup: Cady asks to be taken to the back building for health class
jokes.punchline: Janis reveals the building burned down — a totally matter-of-fact delivery that makes clear she's been manipulating Cady into skipping
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of a fact that retroactively reveals the entire walk was a con is satisfying comedy. The specific year — 1987 — adds mock-authority. Economy is excellent: five words, entire scam revealed.

jokes.text: Health class: 'Don't have sex. Because you will get pregnant and die. Don't have sex in the missionary position, don't have sex standing up. Just don't do it, promise? OK, everybody take some rubbers.'
jokes.setup: Janis and Damian have tricked Cady into skipping health class; Cady's voiceover wonders what she missed
jokes.punchline: The health lesson is an absurdist escalation of abstinence-only scare tactics, culminating in the teacher distributing condoms anyway — completely undermining her own message
jokes.explanation: One of the most quoted lines in the film. 'You will get pregnant and die' is a perfect compression of abstinence-scare-tactic logic, made funnier by its specificity and total illogic. The structural button — distributing rubbers after a don't-have-sex speech — is a perfect internal contradiction. High quotability, excellent structure.

jokes.text: 'Why didn't they just keep home-schooling you?' / 'They wanted me to get socialized.' / 'Oh, you'll get socialized, all right. A little slice like you.' / 'What are you talking about?' / 'You're a regulation hottie.'
jokes.setup: Damian asks why Cady is in public school; she explains her parents wanted her socialized
jokes.punchline: Damian's ominous 'you'll get socialized alright' followed by the reveal that he just means she's attractive — 'regulation hottie' — deflates the implied menace
jokes.explanation: Good Damian character moment. The faux-ominous setup is a mild misdirection; the real joke is that 'regulation hottie' is simultaneously funny vocabulary and affectionately delivered. Character-specific to Damian's flamboyant commentator persona.

jokes.text: 'OK, everybody take some rubbers.'
jokes.setup: The health teacher has just delivered an abstinence lecture ending in 'you will get pregnant and die'
jokes.punchline: She then immediately distributes condoms — directly contradicting the entire abstinence message
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the abstinence gag — the teacher distributes condoms in the same breath as her 'don't have sex' speech. The contradiction is the entire joke. Fey gets two laughs from one setup: first the extreme death threat, then the total ideological incoherence.

jokes.text: 'She asked me how to spell "orange".'
jokes.setup: Damian is explaining that Karen Smith is 'one of the dumbest girls you will ever meet'
jokes.punchline: The evidence: Karen asked him how to spell 'orange' — the most basic, common word possible, chosen for maximum illustration of stupidity
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic specificity. Any dumb thing Karen could have asked would be funny, but 'orange' is ideally chosen — it's simple enough to be shocking, common enough that the failure is total. Near-perfect economy: six words do all the work.

jokes.text: 'She's totally rich because her dad invented Toaster Strudel.'
jokes.setup: Damian introduces Gretchen Wieners as a wealthy mean girl
jokes.punchline: The source of wealth is 'Toaster Strudel' — a mundane, slightly ridiculous breakfast pastry as the foundation of a dynasty
jokes.explanation: Brilliant absurdist specificity. The joke isn't just that it's funny — it's that Toaster Strudel is the perfect choice: too pedestrian to be glamorous, specific enough to be real, and it makes Gretchen's wealth both ridiculous and oddly believable. The word 'invented' adds mock-grandeur. This earns its 8+ for the precision of the comedic choice.

jokes.text: 'That's why her hair is so big. It's full of secrets.'
jokes.setup: Damian establishes that Gretchen knows everyone's business
jokes.punchline: The physical explanation for her big hair is that it contains the secrets — a surreal, literal-metaphor punchline delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in modern American comedy. The joke takes a cliché (big hair) and reframes it with absurdist literalism that's simultaneously a character insight, a visual gag, and a perfect non-sequitur. 'Full of secrets' has the rhythm and surprise of a great punchline. It's become a cultural shorthand. This comfortably clears the 8+ threshold — it's comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in wit, economy, and cultural impact.

jokes.text: 'Don't be fooled, because she may seem like your typical selfish, back-stabbing, slut-faced ho-bag. But in reality, she is so much more than that.'
jokes.setup: Janis is warning Cady about Regina George
jokes.punchline: The 'compliment' structure — 'may seem like X, but is so much more' — is inverted: X is already devastating, and 'so much more' makes it worse, not better
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the phrasing mimics a compliment ('so much more than that') while the content escalates the insult. 'Slut-faced ho-bag' is a memorable compound insult, and the juxtaposition with the inspirational-speech framing is sharp irony. The joke is both Tina Fey's satirical instincts and pure Janis voice. Earns its 8+ for structural sophistication.

jokes.text: The 'How do I even begin to explain Regina George?' Greek chorus sequence — multiple students and teachers giving testimonials
jokes.setup: Janis introduces Regina as the queen bee; the film breaks into a documentary-style chorus of testimonials
jokes.punchline: The testimonials escalate absurdly: hair insured for $10,000, car commercials in Japan, meeting John Stamos, then 'one time she punched me in the face. It was awesome.'
jokes.explanation: A formally inventive comedic set piece. The mockumentary/chorus structure parodies celebrity worship and gossip culture. Each escalating detail is carefully chosen — Japan car commercials (celebrity by proxy), John Stamos (specifically dated cultural name), and the punchline 'she punched me in the face. It was awesome.' is the perfect button: total capitulation to the cult of personality. The sequence earns its score as a sustained comedic construction.

jokes.text: The cafeteria map breakdown: 'Asian nerds, cool Asians... unfriendly black hotties... girls who eat their feelings, girls who don't eat anything... sexually active band geeks...'
jokes.setup: Janis and Damian present a social map of the cafeteria to Cady
jokes.punchline: The categories escalate from generic (freshmen, preps) to increasingly specific and absurd sub-groups, culminating in 'sexually active band geeks' and 'the greatest people you will ever meet and the worst'
jokes.explanation: One of the film's key comedic set pieces. The list structure allows escalating specificity — 'Asian nerds / cool Asians' is a sharp social observation, 'girls who eat their feelings' is a perfect coinage, and 'sexually active band geeks' is a great compound joke. The rhythm of the list is well-constructed, and the callback to 'greatest/worst' as the same group is a nice structural button.

jokes.text: 'Is your muffin buttered? Would you like us to assign someone to butter your muffin?'
jokes.setup: A boy approaches Cady claiming to conduct a lunchtime survey
jokes.punchline: The 'survey question' is a crude double entendre delivered with mock-professionalism
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. The bureaucratic framing ('assign someone') is the best part. Not original — the double-entendre survey trick is a familiar comedy device — but it serves its purpose of establishing Jason as a creep before Regina shuts him down.

jokes.text: Regina dresses down Jason: 'You do not come to a party at my house with Gretchen and then scam on some poor, innocent girl right in front of us three days later.' '...Do you wanna have sex with him?' 'No, thank you.' 'Good. So it's settled. So you can go shave your back now. Bye, Jason.'
jokes.setup: Regina intervenes to protect Cady from Jason's harassment
jokes.punchline: Regina's protection is entirely self-serving and proprietary, culminating in the blunt dismissal 'go shave your back now' — an oddly specific physical insult
jokes.explanation: Strong Regina character establishment. The joke is that her 'defense' of Cady is revealed to be entirely about her own social territory ('you do not come to MY house'), and 'go shave your back' is a perfectly targeted dismissal — specific enough to be a real insult, random enough to be funny. Very Regina.

jokes.text: Regina dressing down Jason: 'You do not come to a party at my house with Gretchen and then scam on some poor, innocent girl right in front of us three days later.'
jokes.setup: Regina appears to defend Cady from Jason's harassment
jokes.punchline: Her defense is entirely about her own social rules and territorial grievances — Cady's feelings are incidental
jokes.explanation: Good Regina characterization — the joke is that she's performing protectiveness while actually enforcing her own dominance. 'Poor, innocent girl' is said with the warmth she'll weaponize later. The joke is in the gap between the form (defending a stranger) and the substance (territorial enforcement).

jokes.text: Regina (examining Cady): 'Shut up.' Cady: 'I didn't say anything.'
jokes.setup: Regina is processing the fact that Cady has never been to school before
jokes.punchline: Regina tells Cady to 'shut up' preemptively — a command to stop a response that hasn't happened — revealing she exists in a reality where her commands don't require triggers
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'I didn't say anything' — produce a perfect character reveal. Regina's 'shut up' is an autonomic response to anything surprising; she doesn't even need a stimulus. It perfectly encapsulates her reality-warping social power. High character integration, near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: 'But you're, like, really pretty.' 'Thank you.' 'So you agree.' 'What?' 'You think you're really pretty.'
jokes.setup: Regina pays Cady what appears to be a compliment
jokes.punchline: Regina immediately reframes the thank-you as an admission of vanity — a rhetorical trap that has no good exit
jokes.explanation: One of the best Regina jokes in the film. This is high-craft social manipulation rendered as comedy — the structure is a logical trap (agree = vain, disagree = fishing for compliments), and Regina springs it with casual ease. It's entirely character-specific to Regina and shows her social intelligence as a weapon. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — earns its 8+.

jokes.text: 'So if you're from Africa... why are you white?' 'Oh, my God, Karen, you can't just ask people why they're white.'
jokes.setup: Karen is trying to process that Cady is from Africa
jokes.punchline: Karen's sincere geographic ignorance produces a genuinely dumb question; Regina's correction mimics a politeness lesson while also being funny for applying 'you can't just ask' logic to race
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally quoted lines in the film. Two distinct jokes land simultaneously: Karen's question is a perfect expression of pure, guileless stupidity, and Regina's correction is funny because it uses the syntax of a social etiquette lesson ('you can't just ask people') applied to something that sounds like it should be a civil rights issue but is just... geographic ignorance. Excellent character integration for both. Earns high score for cultural resonance, structural elegance, and genuine originality.

jokes.text: Regina invites Cady to lunch 'every day for the rest of the week' as if bestowing a great honor: 'We wanna invite you to have lunch with us every day for the rest of the week.' Beat. 'Oh, it's OK...' 'Coolness. So we'll see you tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Regina makes a show of offering Cady a 'really huge deal' invitation
jokes.punchline: The invitation is for the rest of the week — a few days — presented with the gravity of a lifetime honor; and when Cady starts to decline, Regina simply ignores her
jokes.explanation: Good Regina character comedy — the gap between the solemnity of 'this is a really huge deal' and the actual offer (a few lunches) is the joke, plus she doesn't hear Cady's refusal. Efficient character work.

jokes.text: 'On Wednesdays, we wear pink.'
jokes.setup: Regina finishes delivering the terms of the lunch invitation
jokes.punchline: Karen adds this rule as if it is of equal or greater importance to everything else — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Five words that became one of the most quoted lines in pop culture. The genius is structural: it arrives immediately after the pompous invitation, treating a dress code rule as a binding social law. Karen's earnest delivery is crucial — it's funny because SHE isn't joking. Extremely high quotability, strong character integration, near-perfect economy. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: 'Regina George is not sweet. She's a scum-sucking road whore! She ruined my life!'
jokes.setup: Cady naively says 'Regina seems sweet' after spending five minutes with her
jokes.punchline: Janis erupts with 'scum-sucking road whore' — a wildly escalated response delivered with genuine personal trauma
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'Regina seems sweet' and 'scum-sucking road whore' is enormous and funny. The specificity of 'road whore' (not just 'whore') is Fey's fingerprint. Janis's immediate escalation to 'she ruined my life' hints at real backstory, adding a layer of tragicomedy.

jokes.text: 'Why do you hate her?' / 'Yes. What's your question?'
jokes.setup: Cady asks 'Why do you hate her?' as a simple question
jokes.punchline: Janis responds to 'why do you hate her?' as if it's already established fact and asks for the actual question — confirming her hatred is a given, not up for discussion
jokes.explanation: Smart, economical joke. By responding 'Yes. What's your question?' Janis skips past any defensiveness about hating Regina and treats it as established fact, asking only for the specific inquiry. It's a clever rhetorical move that's also very funny. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: "Oh my God, Danny DeVito! I love your work!" — Damian spots Ms. Norbury at the mall
jokes.setup: The group spots Ms. Norbury (their teacher) shopping at the mall
jokes.punchline: Damian greets a plain, middle-aged woman at a soap store as if she's Danny DeVito
jokes.explanation: Absurdist non-sequitur that works on multiple levels: it's random enough to be funny, specific enough (Danny DeVito, not just 'some celebrity') to be great, and characterizes Damian perfectly. The 'I love your work' earnestness sells it.

jokes.text: Girl World rules: 'You can't wear a tank top two days in a row, and you can only wear your hair in a ponytail once a week. So I guess you picked today.' / 'Oh, and we only wear jeans or track pants on Fridays. Now, if you break any of these rules, you can't sit with us at lunch.'
jokes.setup: Cady is introduced to the rules of 'Girl World'
jokes.punchline: The rules are absurdly specific and delivered with the gravity of constitutional law; Gretchen's aside about the ponytail ('so I guess you picked today') targets Cady with passive-aggressive precision
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe comedy. The rules themselves are satirically sharp observations about real teenage girl behavior, magnified to absurdity. Gretchen's delivery — solemn as a legal reading — is essential. The rewatch bonus comes from noticing how Cady's future rule-breaking pays this off.

jokes.text: 'OK, like, if I was wearing jeans today, I would be sitting over there with the art freaks.' [Gretchen gestures; Cady looks over]
jokes.setup: Gretchen is explaining the dress-code consequences
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: Gretchen pointing to the art freaks table with casual condescension, treating denim as a one-way ticket to social exile
jokes.explanation: Modest but functional character comedy. The visual of Gretchen gesturing to the 'art freaks' as a threat amplifies the absurdity of the dress code stakes. Not exceptional but serves the satirical world-building.

jokes.text: 'Well, I mean, you wouldn't buy a skirt without asking your friends first if it looks good on you.' 'I wouldn't?'
jokes.setup: Gretchen explains the rule that you must consult the group about guys, like consulting friends about clothes
jokes.punchline: Cady's simple 'I wouldn't?' — genuine bafflement at a behavior presented as universal — reveals how alien this world is to her
jokes.explanation: Economical character beat. Cady's outsider status does the work here — the assumption embedded in Gretchen's rule is exposed as not universal by a simple two-word question.

jokes.text: Regina calculates: 'A hundred and twenty calories and 48 calories from fat. What percent is that?' Cady solves it instantly. 'It's 40 percent.' 'Whatever. I'm getting cheese fries.'
jokes.setup: Regina performs a nutritional calculation ritual before eating, implying obsessive diet consciousness
jokes.punchline: Despite learning the food is 40% fat (above her stated 30% limit), she immediately abandons the calculation and orders cheese fries — the whole exercise was performance, not discipline
jokes.explanation: Smart character comedy. The setup frames Regina as a disciplined dieter; the punchline reveals the whole ritual is theatrical. It also shows Cady's math skill while simultaneously making the math irrelevant to Regina, which is a layered joke. 'Whatever. I'm getting cheese fries.' is delivered with zero self-awareness — classic Regina.

jokes.text: Gretchen doing nutrition math at the table: 'A hundred and twenty calories, 48 from fat, what percent is that?' — Cady correctly solves it, Gretchen ignores the math and gets cheese fries
jokes.setup: Gretchen is performing dietary vigilance by calculating fat percentages
jokes.punchline: After Cady correctly walks through the cross-multiplication, Gretchen simply says 'Whatever. I'm getting cheese fries.' — the entire exercise was performative
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about the performative nature of diet culture. The elaborate math setup is revealed as meaningless — the decision to get cheese fries was always going to happen. The gap between the analytic rigor (cross-multiplication, the value of X) and 'Whatever, cheese fries' is the entire joke. Also does good setup work for Cady's math competence.

jokes.text: 'OK, irregardless. Ex-boyfriends are just off-limits to friends. I mean, that's just, like, the rules of feminism.'
jokes.setup: Gretchen is establishing that Aaron Samuels is off-limits
jokes.punchline: She uses 'irregardless' (not a word) and attributes boyfriend territorial rules to 'the rules of feminism' — a complete misunderstanding of feminism delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the best Gretchen jokes in the film. 'Irregardless' establishes her as someone who confidently misuses language, then 'the rules of feminism' takes it to another level — it's not just wrong, it's the specific opposite of what feminism means, and she deploys it as a trump card for proprietary control over a boy. Pure Gretchen voice, completely original social observation, and the double comedic payload (malapropism + ideological inversion) is Tina Fey at her best. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: 'Don't worry. I'll never tell Regina what you said.' CUT TO: 'I know your secret.'
jokes.setup: Gretchen solemnly promises to keep Cady's crush on Aaron a secret
jokes.punchline: Instant cut to Regina calling Cady and announcing she knows the secret — Gretchen told immediately
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural irony. The juxtaposition is instantaneous — the edit itself is the joke. Gretchen's solemn assurance makes the betrayal funnier, and it confirms what the film has established about her as a gossip. The 'just established' callback structure is used at maximum efficiency. Earns its 8+ for structural elegance.

jokes.text: 'Don't worry. I'll never tell Regina what you said.' — immediately cut to Regina knowing exactly what Cady said
jokes.setup: Gretchen promises Cady she'll keep the Aaron crush secret
jokes.punchline: Regina immediately confronts Cady on the phone with the information — the secret lasted approximately zero time
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony played for laughs. The speed of the betrayal — Gretchen promises, then the film cuts directly to the consequence — is the craft. The audience needs no scene of Gretchen telling Regina; the cut says everything. Good structural filmmaking as comedy delivery.

jokes.text: Cady pretends to be lost in calculus to talk to Aaron; voiceover: 'But I wasn't lost. I knew exactly what Ms. Norbury was talking about.' / Aaron explains it wrong / 'Wrong. He was so wrong.'
jokes.setup: Cady feigns confusion in calculus to have an excuse to talk to Aaron Samuels
jokes.punchline: Aaron's explanation is wrong. Cady's voiceover confirms it with 'Wrong. He was so wrong.' — she is letting a cute boy explain math incorrectly to her
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the joke has two movements. First, Cady's pretense is exposed to the audience (not Aaron) creating dramatic irony. Then the kicker: Aaron is wrong, and Cady knows it, and she's thanking him anyway. The double standard of a genuinely intelligent person playing dumb for a boy who is both wrong AND condescending is a pointed joke about gender dynamics in STEM disguised as a cute rom-com beat. 'Wrong. He was so wrong.' is a satisfying and funny button.

jokes.text: "Being at Old Orchard Mall kind of reminded me of being home in Africa. By the watering hole... when the animals are in heat." [Visual: glamorous/predatory teens at the mall]
jokes.setup: Cady is at the mall with The Plastics for the first time
jokes.punchline: She compares the mall social scene to an African watering hole in mating season — Cady's zoologist-family background producing a deadpan nature-documentary framing for teenage social behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the thematically richest jokes in this reel. Cady's Africa/zoologist background — established earlier — pays off perfectly here with a nature-documentary lens applied to suburban teen social dynamics. 'When the animals are in heat' is specific, funny, and genuinely insightful satire. High character integration (only Cady could make this observation), strong economy, and it establishes the film's central satirical metaphor. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Regina calls Taylor Wedell's house posing as Susan from Planned Parenthood with 'urgent test results'
jokes.setup: Regina discovers Jason is at the mall with Taylor Wedell and decides to intervene
jokes.punchline: She impersonates a Planned Parenthood worker with fake 'urgent test results' — an elaborately cruel prank executed with casual expert precision
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny — the prank is mean-spirited enough to be transgressive and clever enough to be impressive. Regina's ease and confidence executing it instantly characterizes her as someone who does this routinely. The specific 'Susan from Planned Parenthood' detail is well-chosen.

jokes.text: 'She's not going out with anyone.' 'OK, that was so fetch.'
jokes.setup: Regina finishes the prank call; Gretchen reacts
jokes.punchline: Gretchen uses 'fetch' — her England-imported slang — to praise the cruelty, which is funny because the word is aggressively uncool applied to genuinely dark behavior
jokes.explanation: First use of 'fetch' in a callback context — sets up the running gag that Regina will shut down. Light joke on its own, but important as running gag infrastructure.

jokes.text: Regina's little sister watches TV — implicitly while Regina and her mom engage in their dynamic
jokes.setup: The family arrives home; a younger girl is watching TV
jokes.punchline: The younger sister appears to be watching something inappropriate (the content of which is implied) with complete nonchalance — establishing the household's total lack of supervision
jokes.explanation: A quick visual background joke establishing the George household's chaotic permissiveness. Functional but not developed enough to be more than a minor beat. Sets up Mrs. George's character.

jokes.text: 'Make sure you check out her mom's boob job. They're hard as rocks.'
jokes.setup: The girls arrive at Regina's house; Gretchen offers Cady a tour tip
jokes.punchline: Gretchen matter-of-factly recommends inspecting Mrs. George's breast augmentation as a point of interest — delivered as a helpful orientation note
jokes.explanation: Light cringe comedy that sets up Mrs. George's introduction. The casualness of the tip is the joke — it's delivered as standard welcoming advice. 'Hard as rocks' is a specific detail that sells the joke.

jokes.text: 'Just want you to know, if you need anything, don't be shy, OK? There are no rules in this house. I'm not like a regular mom. I'm a cool mom. Right, Regina?' 'Please stop talking.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. George welcomes Cady to the house with excessive friendliness
jokes.punchline: Her self-designation as a 'cool mom' — the hallmark of someone desperately uncool — is immediately deflated by Regina's weary 'Please stop talking'
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not like a regular mom. I'm a cool mom.' is one of the film's most quotable lines. The joke operates on a perfect irony: the act of declaring yourself a 'cool mom' is definitionally uncool, and Mrs. George's oblivious enthusiasm makes it funnier. Regina's 'Please stop talking' is the ideal button — exhausted, not angry. Earns 8+ for quotability and cultural impact.

jokes.text: 'This is your room?' / 'It was my parents' room, but I made them trade me.'
jokes.setup: Cady sees Regina's enormous bedroom
jokes.punchline: Regina explains she simply made her parents give her the master bedroom — delivered as the most natural thing in the world
jokes.explanation: Economical character revelation. The joke is entirely in the delivery — 'I made them trade me' is said without any drama, implying this was a straightforward negotiation that Regina won. Establishes the household power dynamic.

jokes.text: 'Cady, do you even know who sings this?' 'The Spice Girls?' 'I love her. She's like a Martian.'
jokes.setup: Regina puts on music and Karen tests Cady on pop culture
jokes.punchline: Cady guesses wrong (The Spice Girls); Regina's response — 'I love her. She's like a Martian.' — is an insult framed as a compliment, delivered with genuine affection for the strangeness
jokes.explanation: Light but efficient. 'She's like a Martian' is a good Regina line — simultaneously fascinated and dismissive. The Spice Girls guess establishes Cady's pop culture gap without belaboring it.

jokes.text: Body-shaming mirror sequence: 'God, my hips are huge!' / 'I hate my calves.' / 'I've got man shoulders.' / 'My hairline is so weird.' / 'My pores are huge.' / 'My nail beds suck.' — Cady has nothing to contribute
jokes.setup: The Plastics stand at the mirror cataloguing their physical flaws
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from body parts to increasingly microscopic concerns ('nail beds'), while Cady — who has never done this before — is left with nothing to contribute, staring blankly
jokes.explanation: One of Fey's best satirical sequences. The joke is structural and social: these conventionally beautiful girls perform self-loathing as a bonding ritual, and the game requires a contribution. Cady's outsider status means she has nothing — she hasn't been taught to hate her body yet. 'I used to think there was just fat and skinny. Apparently there's a lot of things that can be wrong on your body.' is a perfect voiceover button that makes the satire explicit without killing the joke. The escalation to 'my nail beds suck' is the comedic peak.

jokes.text: Body-criticism escalation: 'God, my hips are huge!' / 'Oh, please. I hate my calves.' / 'At least you guys can wear halters. I've got man shoulders.' / 'My hairline is so weird.' / 'My pores are huge.' / 'My nail beds suck.' [Cady: 'I used to think there was just fat and skinny. Apparently, there's a lot of things that can be wrong on your body.']
jokes.setup: The Plastics stand in front of a mirror and start cataloguing their flaws
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from common complaints to increasingly specific and obscure body anxieties, culminating in 'my nail beds suck'; Cady's outside observer conclusion ('apparently there's a lot of things that can be wrong on your body') is the comedic button
jokes.explanation: One of the best set pieces in the reel. The escalation from 'my hips are huge' (relatable) to 'my nail beds suck' (completely obscure) is a perfect comedic arc. The joke works on multiple levels: satire of teen body image culture, character development (even Plastics are insecure), and Cady's naive conclusion ('I used to think there was just fat and skinny') is both funny and devastating. 'My nail beds suck' earns its own laugh for sheer specificity. The sequence earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Cady stares at the mirror, clearly having nothing to contribute to the body-criticism session. Awkward beat. Then: 'I have really bad breath in the morning.'
jokes.setup: The Plastics are bonding by criticizing their bodies; there's social pressure on Cady to participate
jokes.punchline: After a beat, Cady offers the only self-criticism she can think of: bad morning breath — a functional flaw, not a vanity complaint, completely missing the point of the ritual
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-based joke. Cady's contribution — 'I have really bad breath in the morning' — is funny because it breaks the ritual's logic entirely. The others are performing anxiety about beauty; Cady offers a pedestrian hygiene complaint. The awkward beat before it heightens the incongruity. It tells us everything about Cady's outsider status in one line, with excellent economy and strong character integration. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Mrs. George knocks on the door: 'Hey, you guys. Happy hour is from 4 to 6!' The girls say 'Thanks.' Then Cady: 'Is there alcohol in this?' Mrs. George: 'Oh, God, honey, no. What kind of mother do you think I am?' [Beat] 'Do you want a bit? If you're gonna drink, I'd rather you do it in the house.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. George brings the girls drinks during 'happy hour'; Cady asks if there's alcohol
jokes.punchline: Mrs. George is offended by the question — 'What kind of mother do you think I am?' — then immediately offers to let Cady drink in the house, completely undermining her own defense
jokes.explanation: Classic callback structure within a single joke: Mrs. George's rhetorical question 'What kind of mother do you think I am?' is answered by her immediate offer to enable underage drinking. Excellent structure — setup, false resolution, undercut. Deepens the 'cool mom' characterization established earlier.

jokes.text: 'Is there alcohol in this?' / 'Oh, God, honey, no. What kind of mother do you think I am? ... Do you want a bit? If you're gonna drink, I'd rather you do it in the house.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. George brings the girls drinks; Cady asks if there's alcohol
jokes.punchline: Mrs. George is offended by the suggestion — then immediately offers Cady alcohol in the same breath
jokes.explanation: One of the best Mrs. George moments and a structurally perfect joke. The outrage ('What kind of mother do you think I am?') followed immediately by the offer is a beautiful comedic reversal — she is the exact kind of mother Cady thought she was, in real time. The speed of the turnaround is everything; there's no scene break, no hesitation, just one breath of offended dignity and then 'do you want a bit?' Perfect character integration — this IS Mrs. George.

jokes.text: 'What is the 411? What has everybody been up to? What is the hot gossip? Tell me everything. What are you guys listening to? What's the cool jams?' / 'Mom. Could you go fix your hair?'
jokes.setup: Mrs. George wants to be part of the girls' conversation
jokes.punchline: Regina dismisses her with the condescension of a popular girl to an uncool peer — 'Could you go fix your hair?' — treating her own mother like an intrusive classmate
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe comedy. Mrs. George's spray of teen-vernacular phrases ('411,' 'hot gossip,' 'cool jams') is a perfect catalogue of a parent trying too hard. Regina's response — 'Could you go fix your hair?' — is funny because it's a dismissal one would give to an annoying classmate, not a mother. The power inversion is complete.

jokes.text: The Burn Book: 'Trang Pak is a grotsky little byotch.' 'Still true.' / 'Dawn Schweitzer is a fat virgin.' 'Still half true.'
jokes.setup: Regina shows Cady the Burn Book — a scrapbook of insults about every girl in the grade
jokes.punchline: The updates — 'still true' and 'still half true' — treat the insults as ongoing assessments, with 'still half true' implying one part has changed (she's no longer a virgin)
jokes.explanation: 'Still half true' is the best joke here — the implication is efficiently conveyed without saying it. 'Grotsky little byotch' (the phonetic spelling of 'bitch') is a funny stylistic choice for the Burn Book. Dark but precisely crafted.

jokes.text: 'Amber D'Alessio. She made out with a hot dog.'
jokes.setup: Regina is showing Cady entries from the Burn Book
jokes.punchline: The accusation is not that Amber did something with a person — it's that she 'made out with a hot dog,' a grotesque and specific non-sexual object
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the hot dog — not some vague scandal, but this exact item — is what makes it work. It's dark and absurd simultaneously, and the deadpan reading with no additional commentary is perfect economy.

jokes.text: Burn Book entry 'Janis Ian — dyke.' Cady: 'Who is that?' / 'I think that's that kid Damian.' / 'Yeah. He's almost too gay to function.' / 'That's funny. Put that in there.' / Beat. Cady's reaction: 'Oh, no. Maybe that was only OK when Janis said it.'
jokes.setup: The Plastics misidentify Damian in the yearbook photo and repeat Janis's earlier line about him
jokes.punchline: Regina wants to add 'almost too gay to function' to the Burn Book — the same line that was affectionate when Janis said it becomes an insult in Regina's hands; Cady's internal reaction acknowledges the difference
jokes.explanation: Structurally sophisticated callback. The same line — 'almost too gay to function' — is now recontextualized: affectionate from a friend, weaponized by an enemy. Cady's internal observation ('maybe that was only OK when Janis said it') is a sharp ethical observation delivered as a small internal joke. The recontextualization is the comedic AND thematic payload. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Janis: 'There are two kinds of evil people. People who do evil stuff, and people who see evil stuff being done and don't try to stop it.' [Cady's immediate reaction shot]: 'Does that mean I'm morally obligated to burn that lady's outfit?'
jokes.setup: Janis is delivering a genuinely earnest moral argument to Cady about why she should steal the Burn Book
jokes.punchline: Cady completely deflates the moral gravity by applying the logic to a random stranger's bad outfit — a perfect literal-minded non-sequitur that demonstrates she's not quite following
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection: Janis builds to a serious ethical point; Cady applies it to fashion police duty. It's funny both as character comedy (Cady's literal-mindedness) and as a deflation of Janis's moral grandstanding. The non-sequitur is precisely calibrated — 'burn that lady's outfit' applies the moral framework sincerely and absurdly simultaneously.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my God, that's Ms. Norbury. I love seeing teachers outside of school. It's like seeing a dog walk on its hind legs.'
jokes.setup: The group spots Ms. Norbury at the mall
jokes.punchline: Damian's simile — a teacher outside school is like a dog walking on hind legs — is a vivid, perfect articulation of a universal childhood/teen experience
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable and original observational jokes in the film. The simile is perfectly chosen — 'a dog walk on its hind legs' captures both the uncanniness and the delighted surprise of seeing a teacher in the real world. It's a universal experience elevated by an extraordinary specific image. Near-flawless economy. High originality for finding the perfect comparison. Earns its 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Ms. Norbury: 'No, I'm just here with my boyfriend.' Beat. 'Joking. Sometimes older people make jokes.'
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury explains why she's at the mall (she works there part-time); she adds 'just here with my boyfriend'
jokes.punchline: She immediately flags it as a joke and adds the meta-commentary 'sometimes older people make jokes' — poking fun at her own divorced, dateless status while also breaking the fourth wall slightly
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware Ms. Norbury joke. The structure is a fake-out followed by over-explanation, which is itself funny — the extra step of saying 'sometimes older people make jokes' is both slightly pathetic and self-aware. The callback to her earlier 'I got divorced' makes it land harder.

jokes.text: 'My nana takes her wig off when she's drunk.' Ms. Norbury: 'Your nana and I have that in common.'
jokes.setup: Damian offers a random personal anecdote about his grandmother
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury immediately claims the same behavior — suggesting she also removes her wig when drunk — delivered with the deadpan of someone who has nothing left to lose
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and Ms. Norbury character work. The joke requires Tina Fey's specific brand of resigned, self-deprecating humor. The randomness of the nana anecdote sets up the teacher's unexpected self-identification with the same behavior. Good deadpan structure.

jokes.text: 'Well, this has been sufficiently awkward.'
jokes.setup: An extended awkward encounter in the soap shop ends
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury names the social discomfort of the entire scene with 'sufficiently awkward' — a perfectly calibrated assessment that is itself elegantly awkward
jokes.explanation: The word 'sufficiently' is doing all the work here — not 'pretty awkward' or 'very awkward,' but a formal measurement: it has reached the required threshold of awkward and may now be dismissed. Very economical and completely in Norbury's voice.

jokes.text: Cady gets a call: 'I know your secret.' — her panicked internal monologue: 'Oh God, busted. Just start apologizing and crying. No, play it cool.' — it's just about Aaron Samuels
jokes.setup: Cady receives a call from an unknown voice saying 'I know your secret,' and her internal monologue catastrophizes
jokes.punchline: The 'secret' is merely that she likes Aaron — the most mundane teenage secret — not the spy operation
jokes.explanation: Good sustained misdirection. The audience assumes 'secret' = spy mission; the reveal is anticlimactic in a funny way. Cady's frantic internal deliberation ('Just start apologizing and crying. No, play it cool.') is a good window into her character — she's genuinely good-hearted and worried about being caught doing something wrong.

jokes.text: Regina's three-way call trap: 'Aren't you so mad at Gretchen for telling me?' / (to Gretchen, switching ears): 'See, Gretch? I told you she's not mad at you.' / 'I can't believe you think I like attention!'
jokes.setup: Regina is on a three-way call, secretly with both Cady and Gretchen listening
jokes.punchline: Regina harvests quotes from Cady to weaponize against Gretchen in real-time — a masterclass in social manipulation revealed in one phone call, culminating in Gretchen's oblivious outburst
jokes.explanation: One of the most structurally sophisticated jokes in this reel. The three-way call allows Regina to play both parties simultaneously — it's a comedic revelation of her social engineering genius. Cady's voiceover ('I had survived my first three-way calling attack') frames it perfectly. The punchline — Gretchen's wounded 'I can't believe you think I like attention!' — is funny because it completely misses the real dynamic. High character integration, clever structure.

jokes.text: Regina's three-way call trap — 'See, Gretch? I told you she's not mad at you.' / 'I can't believe you think I like attention!'
jokes.setup: Regina has orchestrated a three-way call where Cady doesn't know Gretchen is listening; she maneuvers Cady into saying Gretchen 'likes attention'
jokes.punchline: Regina immediately reveals Gretchen is on the line by calling out to her — Gretchen's reaction is to be offended by the 'attention' characterization, not by being manipulated
jokes.explanation: One of the best Regina scenes in the film. The three-way call is a classic teen social weapon and Fey executes the reveal with perfect timing. The real joke is Gretchen's reaction: she doesn't react to being used as a pawn in a manipulation scheme, she reacts to being called attention-seeking. Her total blindness to the larger manipulation while being hyperaware of the specific slight is a perfect character portrait. 'OK, love you, see you tomorrow' as Regina's breezy exit after causing chaos is chef's kiss character writing.

jokes.text: On October 3rd, Aaron asks Cady what day it is. 'It's October 3rd.' / Two weeks later: 'It's raining.' / 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover announces that she and Aaron started talking more, implying growing romance
jokes.punchline: Their actual conversations are: (1) Aaron asks what day it is, Cady answers; (2) two weeks later, Aaron notes it's raining, Cady agrees. That's the relationship.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film. Fey takes the romantic comedy convention of 'and then we started talking' and reveals the actual content of teenage romantic 'connection' — an exchange about the date, then a weather observation two weeks later. The gap between Cady's romantic narration and the mundane reality is funny and emotionally true. 'It's October 3rd' became one of the most quoted lines in the film precisely because it's so perfect in its specificity and anti-climax. 'On October 3rd, he asked me what day it was' is a sentence that only makes sense as a love story, which is the entire joke.

jokes.text: Aaron gives Cady his number: 'That flier admits one person only, so don't bring some other guy with you.' Cady's reaction: 'Grool.' / 'I meant to say cool and then I started to say great.' / 'Right. Well... grool.'
jokes.setup: Aaron invites Cady to a party and gives her his number; Cady tries to respond coolly
jokes.punchline: She produces a portmanteau of 'great' and 'cool' — 'grool' — tries to explain it, and Aaron graciously repeats it back, which is both endearing and mortifying
jokes.explanation: Perfect cringe comedy — Cady's collision of words captures the exact panic of trying to be cool in front of a crush. 'Grool' is funny as a word, funnier still as an accidental invention, and Aaron's gentle '...grool' is both sweet and mortifying. High character integration.

jokes.text: Cady's voiceover: 'In the regular world, Halloween is when children dress up in costumes and beg for candy. In Girl World, Halloween is the one night a year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it. The hard-core girls just wear lingerie and some form of animal ears.'
jokes.setup: Cady is preparing for a Halloween party
jokes.punchline: The 'regular world' vs. 'Girl World' framing renders the Halloween costume phenomenon as an anthropological observation, culminating in the anthropologically precise 'some form of animal ears'
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally quotable monologues in the film and in pop culture broadly. The 'regular world' vs. 'Girl World' framing is Cady's signature observational lens — which only she can deliver because of her Africa background — and the analysis of Halloween costumes as a sanctioned slut loophole is both genuinely insightful sociology and excellent comedy. 'Some form of animal ears' is the perfect precision detail. Earns its 8+ for originality, cultural impact, and character integration.

jokes.text: 'In the regular world, Halloween is when children dress up in costumes and beg for candy. In Girl World, Halloween is the one night a year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it.'
jokes.setup: Cady is preparing for a Halloween party
jokes.punchline: Her outsider anthropological frame recontextualizes Halloween as specifically a sanctioned sluttiness window — which is both funny and culturally accurate
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally resonant jokes in the film — the 'Halloween is a slut pass' observation became a widely cited cultural shorthand. Fey delivers it through Cady's anthropological narrator voice, which makes the pointed social commentary feel like scientific observation rather than judgment. 'No other girls can say anything about it' captures the specific social logic perfectly. This is excellent observational comedy at the border of satire.

jokes.text: Mom asks: 'Doesn't she look great, honey?' [Cady is apparently in a mouse costume (ears) with lingerie.] 'What are you?' 'I'm a mouse.' Cut to Halloween party reveal: Cady has shown up in a full zombie bride costume, while everyone else wears lingerie and ears.
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover has just established the 'lingerie + animal ears' rule for Halloween in Girl World; Cady's mom approves of her costume
jokes.punchline: Cady arrives at the party in a full head-to-toe zombie costume — 'nobody told me about the slut rule' — a perfect visual payoff to the setup, and the gap between her costume and everyone else's is entirely visual
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. The voiceover setup (30 seconds earlier) is immediately undercut by the visual reveal. The 'I'm a mouse' at home — which sounds like the right answer — sets up the expectation that she got it, then the party reveals she interpreted it too literally (or entirely missed the memo). The final line 'unfortunately, no one told me about the slut rule' is a great button. High structure score for the compact setup-to-payoff efficiency.

jokes.text: Cady arrives at the party in a full zombie/scary costume; everyone else is in lingerie and animal ears. 'What are you?' / 'I'm a mouse.'
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover has just explained the Halloween 'slut rule'; she says 'unfortunately, no one told me about the slut rule'
jokes.punchline: She arrives in a full costume (zombie bride, implied) among dozens of girls in lingerie, then someone in lingerie-and-ears identifies her costume as 'a mouse'
jokes.explanation: Perfect visual payoff to a verbal setup. The gap between the full zombie costume and the lingerie crowd is a visual joke that lands entirely in the image. The added layer: a girl in lingerie (arguably wearing very little costume) identifies herself as 'a mouse,' which is funny on its own — the mouse ears do not constitute a costume, but within Girl World they absolutely do. The juxtaposition of Cady's elaborate monster makeup against someone who considers lingerie + mouse ears a 'costume' is the whole movie in a single image.

jokes.text: Why are you dressed so scary? / It's Halloween.
jokes.setup: Karen asks a partygoer why they're dressed 'so scary,' implying she doesn't understand costume parties
jokes.punchline: The answer is simply 'It's Halloween' — Karen's obliviousness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Karen joke — she asks something that reveals she doesn't understand a basic social concept. The economy is excellent (four words, one beat) and it's well integrated into her established airhead character, though it's not a high-tier gag.

jokes.text: He's your cousin. / Yeah, but he's my FIRST cousin.
jokes.setup: Karen admits she thinks Seth Mosakowski is a good kisser; someone points out he's her cousin
jokes.punchline: Karen doubles down with the distinction of 'first cousin,' implying she thinks that makes it MORE acceptable, then attempts a confusing taxonomy of cousin types
jokes.explanation: The escalation is perfectly structured: Karen's defense of kissing a cousin by clarifying he's her FIRST cousin — implying closeness makes it okay rather than worse — is a great inversion of logic. The failed cousin-taxonomy extension ('you have your cousins, then your first cousins, then your second cousins...') adds a second beat that lands. Very Karen-specific humor.

jokes.text: And you are... a zombie bride. / An 'ex-wife.'
jokes.setup: Aaron guesses Cady's Halloween costume is a zombie bride
jokes.punchline: Cady corrects him — she's an 'ex-wife' — reframing the horror costume as a social commentary punchline
jokes.explanation: Clean one-beat joke with excellent economy. The misdirection works because 'zombie bride' is the obvious guess and 'ex-wife' reframes the same visual as bitter marital comedy. Not deeply character-specific for Cady but it's a sharp line.

jokes.text: Regina's fabricated story about Cady: the T-shirt, the Kleenex voodoo, 'Mrs. Aaron Samuels' in her notebook
jokes.setup: Regina tells Aaron she wants to help Cady, framing it as a favor while secretly sabotaging her
jokes.punchline: The lies escalate absurdly: Cady writes 'Mrs. Aaron Samuels' in her notebook → wears an 'I heart Aaron' shirt under her clothes → saved his used Kleenex → plans African voodoo with it
jokes.explanation: This is a showcase for Regina's particular brand of malice dressed as friendship. Each escalating lie is funnier than the last — from notebook doodling (relatable) to a T-shirt worn under clothes (obsessive) to Kleenex voodoo (unhinged). The structure is excellent: she always prefixes with 'I'm not saying...' while saying exactly that. Deeply character-specific. The African voodoo gag lands because it's the most absurd and also reveals Regina's own casual racism.

jokes.text: So just promise me you won't make fun of her. / Of course I'm not gonna make fun of her. / How could Janis hate Regina? She was such a good... SLUT!
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover marvels that Janis could hate Regina, who is performing such warmth — 'She was such a good...'
jokes.punchline: The voiceover is interrupted mid-sentence by someone off-screen yelling 'Slut!' at Regina, completing the sentence in the most damning way possible
jokes.explanation: One of the best-constructed jokes in this reel. The setup is a classic dramatic irony moment — Cady's naive voiceover ('She was such a good...') is set up to deliver a compliment, but the edit intercepts it with a random partygoer screaming 'Slut!' The timing, the visual juxtaposition of Regina's sweet act with the external verdict, and the sentence completion structure are all working in perfect harmony. Economical, structurally elegant, deeply rewatchable. Easily an 8+ moment.

jokes.text: What are you doing? You broke up with me. / That's crazy. Why would I break up with you? You're so hot.
jokes.setup: Aaron is confused because Regina dumped him; she's now acting like it never happened
jokes.punchline: Regina's reason for not breaking up with him is entirely appearance-based ('You're so hot') — a perfect encapsulation of her shallow worldview delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Regina's complete rewriting of history is very her, and 'you're so hot' as the sole justification for reversing a breakup is nicely shallow. Not the sharpest joke but it does character work.

jokes.text: That's a scary mask, bro. (said to Aaron's natural face)
jokes.setup: It's a Halloween party; someone presumably mistakes Aaron's real face for a costume mask
jokes.punchline: Aaron is not wearing a mask — the insult is delivered deadpan as a compliment/costume comment
jokes.explanation: Quick throwaway gag that plays on Halloween costume confusion as a backhanded insult to Aaron's looks. It's functional but not very specific — could happen to any character and doesn't require the Mean Girls world to work.

jokes.text: Cady's voiceover: 'My stomach felt like it was going to fall out my butt.'
jokes.setup: Cady describes the physical sensation of heartbreak/jealousy watching Regina take Aaron back
jokes.punchline: The list of physical symptoms builds toward poetic ('lump in my throat') but detours into 'my stomach felt like it was going to fall out my butt' — an incongruously crude anatomical image
jokes.explanation: The joke works through tonal contrast — an earnest, slightly poetic description of heartbreak punctuated by a bluntly crude physical image. It's the Tina Fey voice: elevated diction crashing into gross specificity. Not her sharpest but charming.

jokes.text: Because she's a life-ruiner. She ruins people's lives.
jokes.setup: Cady asks why Regina would take Aaron back after hurting her
jokes.punchline: Janis offers the tautological explanation that Regina is 'a life-ruiner' who 'ruins people's lives' — the repetition itself is the joke
jokes.explanation: The circular logic ('she's a life-ruiner / she ruins people's lives') is delivered with complete conviction, as if the redundancy is a profound insight. Very quotable and works as a character beat for Janis's obsessive hatred of Regina. High quotability score because it became a cultural artifact.

jokes.text: Regina George is an evil dictator. Now, how do you overthrow a dictator? You cut off her resources.
jokes.setup: Janis frames their high-school social war in the language of geopolitical strategy
jokes.punchline: The utter seriousness with which she applies dictator-overthrow logic to a teenage girl's social standing, then lists 'high-status man candy' as a resource
jokes.explanation: A solid satirical joke about how seriously teenage social hierarchies mirror political power structures. The gap between 'overthrowing a dictator' and 'popular girl at high school' is the engine. 'High-status man candy' is a great coinage. Consistent with Janis's theatrical personality.

jokes.text: OK, let's rock this bitch.
jokes.setup: Janis has laid out an elaborate strategic plan for destroying Regina's social standing
jokes.punchline: The plan concludes with the maximally casual 'let's rock this bitch' — a tonal whiplash from strategic monologue to blunt profanity
jokes.explanation: A quick button on the strategy scene. The tonal pivot from elaborate political metaphor to casual profanity works, though it's a fairly common comedic beat (elaborate setup, flippant conclusion). Economy is high.

jokes.text: It's called the South Beach Fat Flush, and all you drink is cranberry juice for 72 hours. / This isn't even cranberry juice. It's cranberry juice cocktail. It's all sugar. / I wanna lose 3 pounds.
jokes.setup: Regina gives Cady a 'health' flush diet as a subtle put-down
jokes.punchline: Gretchen immediately fact-checks that it's cranberry juice COCKTAIL (all sugar), which undermines the diet entirely; Regina's response is the already-established 'I wanna lose 3 pounds' — a callback to her body dysmorphia gag from an earlier scene
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: Gretchen's literal fact-checking of the juice cocktail is a funny character beat (she's compulsively helpful even when it undercuts the plan), and 'I wanna lose 3 pounds' as the final word satirizes body image obsession in thin girls. The callback amplifies both.

jokes.text: Why do you wear your hair like that? Your hair looks so sexy pushed back. Cady, will you please tell him his hair looks sexy pushed back.
jokes.setup: Regina compliments Aaron's hair in a way that's simultaneously a put-down of his current style
jokes.punchline: She then demands Cady echo the compliment — using Cady as a puppet to flirt with her own boyfriend in front of Cady, the cruelty is casual and brazen
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the power dynamic — Regina forces Cady to compliment Aaron while Cady has a crush on him, an exquisite cruelty that also sets up the 'your hair looks sexy pushed back' callback later in the reel. Character work more than a pure laugh, but it lands as dark comedy.

jokes.text: Regina was dangling Aaron in front of me on purpose. I knew how this would be settled in the animal world. [Cut to nature footage of two animals fighting] But this was Girl World.
jokes.setup: Cady describes the tension of competing with Regina for Aaron
jokes.punchline: The voiceover pivots to 'I knew how this would be settled in the animal world' — implying direct physical combat — then cuts to actual nature footage, before Cady redirects to the passive-aggressive reality of 'Girl World'
jokes.explanation: One of the film's signature recurring devices — using nature documentary footage to frame high-school social dynamics. The setup-visual cut-redirect structure is tight and original. 'Girl World' as a concept doing satirical work about how female competition is coded as more sophisticated (and in some ways more vicious) than direct combat. This is Fey at her most conceptually sharp in this reel.

jokes.text: All this cranberry juice is making me break out.
jokes.setup: Regina is on the South Beach Fat Flush diet she prescribed Cady — but Cady has secretly been switching the cranberry juice with something else (the face-smelling-like-peppermint gag suggests Cady introduced a skin product)
jokes.punchline: Regina unknowingly reports a symptom of the sabotage she doesn't know is happening — the cranberry juice isn't causing breakouts, but Cady's subtle sabotage is
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained sabotage comedy — Regina attributing the wrong cause to her symptoms is the ironic engine. Works better on rewatch when you understand what Cady's been doing.

jokes.text: Your face smells like peppermint. [Long pause / no explanation given]
jokes.setup: Aaron mentions Regina's face smells like peppermint — a non-sequitur that implies something is off about her skincare routine
jokes.punchline: The comment hangs in the air with no explanation, which is funnier than any explanation would be — the audience knows Cady has sabotaged her products
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the deadpan delivery and the gap — we know why her face smells like peppermint but the characters don't address it. The payoff is fully visual/tonal. High economy score (six words carrying a whole storyline).

jokes.text: This is ass, you guys. It's been a month, and all we've done is make Regina's face smell like a foot.
jokes.setup: Janis reviews the progress of their revenge plan after a month
jokes.punchline: 'All we've done is make Regina's face smell like a foot' — the deflating summary of their grand sabotage plan reduced to a minor sensory inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the sabotage montage. 'Make Regina's face smell like a foot' is a brilliantly specific and deflating summary — not 'we failed,' but we achieved something so minor it's almost worse than nothing. Very high quotability. The specificity of 'foot' rather than any other smell is a good writing choice.

jokes.text: Damian: 'I've been really busy with choir.'
jokes.setup: Cady and Janis are frustrated that the revenge plan has stalled. Damian offers an excuse.
jokes.punchline: 'I've been really busy with choir' — a hilariously inadequate excuse that reveals Damian's priorities and the absurdity of treating revenge like a group project.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat for Damian. The banality of 'choir' as an excuse for failing to destroy the most popular girl in school is absurdly deflating. Only Damian would say this.

jokes.text: Cady: 'Say crack again.' Janis: 'Crack.' — after Janis says 'we gotta crack Gretchen Wieners.'
jokes.setup: Janis uses the word 'crack' in a strategic/metaphorical sense ('crack Gretchen Wieners').
jokes.punchline: Cady's request to 'say crack again' and Janis's flat compliance — a small meta-moment about the absurdity of the word in context.
jokes.explanation: Minor wordplay beat. The double meaning of 'crack' (crack the code / crack cocaine, since Cady later tells Regina that Janis was talking to her 'about crack') sets up a future joke. Moderate payoff on its own.

jokes.text: Regina's story about Janis: 'I was like, Why are you so obsessed with me?' / 'I couldn't have a lesbian at my party. There are gonna be girls there in their bathing suits. I mean, right?'
jokes.setup: Regina tells the 'official' backstory of her falling out with Janis Ian, framing herself as the reasonable victim
jokes.punchline: Regina's logic for excluding Janis from her pool party is delivered with complete sincerity — 'there are gonna be girls there in their bathing suits' — revealing her as both bigoted and obliviously self-incriminating
jokes.explanation: Regina's justification is so casually horrifying that it functions as both character comedy and satire of a certain kind of teenage cruelty. 'Why are you so obsessed with me?' delivered as a reasonable question is a great line — it's her MO throughout the film (narcissism dressed as reasonable concern). The logic of the bathing suit argument is delivered with total conviction, which is funnier than self-awareness would be.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, I love your skirt. Where did you get it? / It was my mom's in the '80s. / Vintage. So adorable. / [Under her breath to Gretchen] That is the ugliest f-ing skirt I've ever seen.
jokes.setup: Regina compliments a passing girl's skirt effusively to her face
jokes.punchline: Immediately turns to Gretchen and delivers the most brutal possible verdict in total contrast
jokes.explanation: One of the defining Mean Girls moments — the speed of the reversal (zero pause between 'so adorable' and 'ugliest f-ing skirt') is pitch perfect. It's pure distilled Regina: weaponized niceness as a cover for contempt. The structure relies on the gap between registers being as extreme as possible, and it delivers. High impact because it crystallizes Regina's entire character in five seconds. Genuinely memorable.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, I love your bracelet. Where did you get it? [Immediately after the skirt moment]
jokes.setup: Regina has just privately savaged the last girl's skirt
jokes.punchline: Without missing a beat she pivots to another girl with the identical effusive opener — 'Oh my God, I love your bracelet' — the speed making it clear this is an automated behavior
jokes.explanation: The immediate repetition of the formula after the skirt reveal is funnier because we now know the template — the callback lands fast. The humor is in how mechanical Regina's social performance is. Good economy.

jokes.text: So are you gonna send any candy canes? / No. I don't send them, I just get them. / So you better send me one, byotch. Love you.
jokes.setup: Discussion of holiday candy cane grams at school
jokes.punchline: Regina establishes she's too important to send candy canes — she only receives them — then immediately demands one from Gretchen while signing off with 'love you' as if the demand was affectionate
jokes.explanation: 'I don't send them, I just get them' is a perfectly calibrated expression of Regina's entitlement. The 'byotch / love you' combination is funny as a Regina-ism — weaponized endearment. Sets up the candy cane payoff scene.

jokes.text: 'Why, Man, he doth bestride the narrow world like a colossus' might translate into 'Why is he so huge and obnoxious?'
jokes.setup: Cady is translating Julius Caesar for class while thinking about her social war with Regina
jokes.punchline: She offers the most reductive, personally applicable paraphrase of Caesar's tyranny possible — implicitly applying it to Regina
jokes.explanation: Setup for the extended Julius Caesar/Regina parallel that pays off in Gretchen's breakdown monologue. This instance is mild — the paraphrase is slightly blunt — but it plants the structural joke.

jokes.text: Taylor Zimmerman? Two for you. Glenn Cocco? Four for you, Glenn Cocco. You go, Glenn Cocco. And none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.
jokes.setup: Damian distributes candy cane grams at the school, reading names and amounts with increasing enthusiasm for Glenn Cocco
jokes.punchline: After building up Glenn Cocco with 'four for you, Glenn Cocco, you go, Glenn Cocco' (a person we never see or know), the final declaration — 'and none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.' — is both the sabotage landing and a perfect deadpan callback to Regina's earlier 'love you / byotch' register
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel by a significant margin. The structure is impeccable: the escalating mystery of Glenn Cocco getting four candy canes with his own enthusiastic mini-celebration ('you go, Glenn Cocco') followed immediately by the brutal 'and none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.' is a masterclass in comedic economy and misdirection. The 'Bye' is crucial — it's dismissive, final, and exactly the right word. Glenn Cocco as a named background nobody who gets four canes while Gretchen gets zero is a perfect absurdist invention. This became one of the most quoted lines in the film. Comparable to the top anchor examples in structure and quotability.

jokes.text: Damian: 'And none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.'
jokes.setup: Damian has delivered candy canes to several people with escalating enthusiasm. The audience (and Gretchen) expects to hear her name.
jokes.punchline: 'And none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.' — the deliberate exclusion delivered with chirpy finality, the 'Bye' making it even more surgical.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — 'And none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.' may be the most economically devastating six-word sentence in the film. The 'Bye' is what elevates it from mean to iconic; it's so casually dismissive. The structure mirrors the previous enthusiasm (four for Glenn Cocco!) to make the exclusion land harder. This is Tina Fey at her best: maximum cruelty delivered with maximum cheerfulness in minimum words. Legitimate 8+ craft.

jokes.text: 'And none for Gretchen Wieners. Bye.'
jokes.setup: Cady has received her candy cane from 'Regina' — the plan is for Regina to publicly snub Gretchen to begin driving a wedge
jokes.punchline: The delivery girl reads the last name: 'none for Gretchen Wieners' — delivered with casual finality and a cheerful 'Bye,' making a social execution feel like a clerical formality
jokes.explanation: Perhaps the single most quotable line in the film and one of the best in Fey's output. The genius is in the 'Bye' — the delivery girl treats a social execution as a routine administrative task. The rhythm is perfect: building list of names → rising expectations for Gretchen → 'none' → 'Bye.' The word 'Bye' adds a breezy, almost sadistic closure that makes the cruelty funny rather than merely cruel. The structure echoes the candy-cane delivery rhythms so the subversion feels earned. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in cultural impact.

jokes.text: Damian performs 'Beautiful' by Christina Aguilera at the talent show with complete sincerity
jokes.setup: High school talent show; Damian is introduced as 'a star on the rise'
jokes.punchline: He performs 'Beautiful' (a female empowerment anthem) with total commitment and apparent emotional investment — the comedy is in the gap between the song choice and his confidence, plus the audience reaction
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Damian's complete sincerity — he's not performing the song as a joke, he genuinely means every word, which makes it funnier than ironic self-awareness would. Character-integrated because only Damian would do this. The extended performance during which Gretchen's breakdown is cross-cut adds to the absurdism.

jokes.text: Maybe she forgot about you. / Yeah, Regina has been acting kind of weird lately. / Well, I mean, her parents totally don't sleep in the same bed anymore, if that's what you mean. / Oh my God. Don't tell her I told you that.
jokes.setup: Cady probes Gretchen about Regina's coldness during the talent show
jokes.punchline: Gretchen immediately volunteers the most intimate family secret — her parents' sleeping arrangements — as if it's a relevant answer, then panics and asks Cady not to repeat it
jokes.explanation: First crack in Gretchen — she can't help oversharing, and the information is family-level private (parents' sleeping arrangements) rather than Regina's social secrets. The 'oh my God, don't tell her I told you' panic is a good button. Establishes the Gretchen-cracking pattern.

jokes.text: No offense, but why would she send you a candy cane? She doesn't even like you that much. / Maybe she feels weird around me because I'm the only person who knows about her nose job.
jokes.setup: Karen (obliviously cruel) questions why Gretchen got a candy cane from Regina; Gretchen defends herself
jokes.punchline: Gretchen accidentally reveals Regina's nose job as her defense mechanism — she thinks this secret gives her value/protection, not realizing she's just given Cady another weapon
jokes.explanation: Karen's 'no offense, but' is a classic Mean Girls construction — the qualifier makes the cruelty explicit. Gretchen's response is perfect character comedy: her only defense is to reveal an even bigger secret, which both proves she has value and confirms she can't keep anything. The escalation of leaking from 'parents' sleeping arrangements' to 'nose job' follows the cracking pattern well.

jokes.text: Kevin G's rap: 'From my grades to my lines / You can't touch Kevin G / I'm a Mathlete / So nerd is inferred / But forget what you heard / I'm like James Bond the Third / Shaken not stirred / I'm Kevin Gnapoor / The G is silent when I sneak in your door / And make love to your woman on the bathroom floor'
jokes.setup: High school talent show; a student identified as a Mathlete takes the stage
jokes.punchline: Kevin G delivers an escalating rap that starts with self-deprecating nerd acknowledgment and climaxes in explicit sexual content at a school talent show, with total confidence
