jokes.explanation: Kevin G's rap works on multiple levels: the rhyme scheme is genuinely clever ('nerd is inferred / forget what you heard / James Bond the Third'), the persona is a great inversion (Mathlete as sexual predator), and the escalation to 'make love to your woman on the bathroom floor' at a school talent show is perfectly inappropriate. 'The G is silent when I sneak in your door' is an inspired wordplay gag. Solid 8 for impact in a room.

jokes.text: K.G. And the Power of Three. That was something. / Does it bother you that they still use your original choreography? / Shut up.
jokes.setup: After Kevin G's performance, the MC gives a vague 'that was something' (meaning: I cannot legally compliment that)
jokes.punchline: Damian pokes Janis by noting the Plastics use 'her original choreography' — implying Janis created the Jingle Bell Rock dance before being expelled from the group — and her response is a defensive 'shut up'
jokes.explanation: 'That was something' is a perfect non-commitment from the MC after Kevin G's inappropriate rap. The Janis choreography reveal is a good piece of comedic world-building that deepens the backstory with Janis/Regina while also being funny on its own.

jokes.text: Gretchen, switch sides with Cady. / But I'm always on your left. / That was when there were three of us, and now the tallest go in the middle. / But the whole dance will be backwards. / I'm always on your left. / And right now you're getting on my last nerve. Switch.
jokes.setup: Regina rearranges the formation backstage before the performance; Gretchen resists based on established habit
jokes.punchline: Gretchen's mounting desperation ('I'm always on your left') is met with Regina's escalating contempt, culminating in 'you're getting on my last nerve.' The cruelty of dismissing a loyal friend's one point of pride in the arrangement is both funny and painful.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy built on the pathos of Gretchen's submission. 'I'm always on your left' as the thing she's willing to fight for, and losing, is sad-funny. Regina's 'that was when there were three of us' is a chilling dismissal. Good character work.

jokes.text: Jason? [The boom box playing the Jingle Bell Rock track skips/breaks mid-performance; Regina glares at someone named Jason in the audience]
jokes.setup: The Plastics are performing their choreographed routine to 'Jingle Bell Rock' in front of the whole school
jokes.punchline: The music cuts out mid-performance; Regina breaks character to glare at Jason (presumably the AV person) with murderous intensity — the gap between the festive performance and her fury is the joke
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the register shift — from synchronized holiday performance to Regina's one-word furious summons. The name 'Jason' is delivered with the weight of a death threat. Good physical/reaction comedy.

jokes.text: During 'Jingle Bell Rock,' the music suddenly cuts out and Cady, in her pink Santa outfit, stares into the crowd and locks eyes with Aaron Samuels. The whole auditorium watches her freeze.
jokes.setup: The Plastics are performing 'Jingle Bell Rock' as a sexy Santa routine. The music cuts out at a critical moment, singling Cady out.
jokes.punchline: Cady freezes completely, staring at Aaron in the audience while silence falls — peak cringe exposure.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cringe — the public humiliation setup works because we know Cady likes Aaron and is now frozen in front of him. The silence is the joke. Primarily visual/performance comedy.

jokes.text: That was the best it ever went! / That was awesome. / Lip gloss.
jokes.setup: The performance included a technical malfunction mid-song
jokes.punchline: Gretchen and Karen celebrate it as 'the best it ever went' and 'awesome' — either in denial, or genuinely unable to see the disaster. Regina's one-word non-response ('Lip gloss') shows her already moving on and not engaging with their enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: The gap between how the performance went and their assessment is the comedy, plus Regina's total disengagement ('Lip gloss'). Regina not even acknowledging their enthusiasm and immediately demanding a cosmetic is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Hey, good job, Africa.
jokes.setup: Aaron compliments Cady after the performance
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'Africa' — using her origin as a nickname — which is both endearing (he remembers where she's from) and mildly absurd (Africa is a continent, not a name)
jokes.explanation: Light gag — 'Africa' as a nickname lands more as a character moment than a big laugh, but it works as quick observational humor. The absurdity of a continent-as-nickname is mild.

jokes.text: That's why you wanted to join the Mathletes. / Mathletes? You hate math. [about Cady's crush on Aaron]
jokes.setup: Regina's group figures out Cady has a crush on Aaron after his compliment
jokes.punchline: Gretchen deduces Cady joined Mathletes because Aaron is in them; Karen blurts that Cady hates math — accidentally confirming the deduction while ostensibly questioning it
jokes.explanation: Functional two-beat joke. Karen's 'Mathletes? You hate math' is good because it both confirms and confuses the accusation simultaneously. Not exceptional but it moves.

jokes.text: That is so fetch. / Gretchen, stop trying to make 'fetch' happen. It's not going to happen.
jokes.setup: Gretchen uses her pet slang word 'fetch' (meaning cool/great)
jokes.punchline: Regina shuts it down with 'stop trying to make fetch happen, it's not going to happen' — a crushing social dismissal of Gretchen's attempt at a contribution to group vocabulary
jokes.explanation: One of the most culturally embedded jokes in the film and in 2000s pop culture. The structure is perfect: 'fetch' is established as a word only Gretchen uses, then Regina destroys it in one sentence that also destroys Gretchen's social ambitions. 'It's not going to happen' is delivered with the finality of a verdict. The irony is that the line itself is making 'fetch' happen — by naming what won't happen, it becomes the most memorable thing in the scene. This approaches the top anchor examples in cultural impact and quotability, scoring just below 'Snip, snap' because of slightly less shocking escalation but comparable economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Gretchen: 'That is so fetch.' Regina: 'Gretchen, stop trying to make fetch happen. It's not going to happen.'
jokes.setup: Gretchen has been trying to introduce 'fetch' as a slang term throughout the film.
jokes.punchline: Regina's flat, final dismissal — 'It's not going to happen' — is simultaneously meta-commentary on trying to force slang into existence and a devastating power play.
jokes.explanation: The single most culturally impactful joke in the film and one of the most quoted lines in 2000s pop culture. 'Stop trying to make fetch happen, it's not going to happen' works on multiple levels: (1) it perfectly characterizes Regina's power over language and social reality, (2) it's self-referential meta-commentary on how slang is made, (3) it's devastatingly dismissive without being technically mean, and (4) the irony is that the line itself BECAME the thing it was dismissing. Highest craft and impact scores in the reel — this is what 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: Gretchen's Caesar monologue: 'Why should Caesar get to stomp around like a giant while the rest of us try not to get smushed under his big feet? What's so great about Caesar? Brutus is just as cute as Caesar...'
jokes.setup: Gretchen is meant to be analyzing Julius Caesar for English class
jokes.punchline: Her 'analysis' is transparently about Regina — 'Brutus is just as CUTE as Caesar,' 'people totally LIKE Brutus just as much as they like Caesar' — culminating in 'We should totally just stab Caesar!' The classroom assignment becomes a barely-veiled breakdown about her own social situation
jokes.explanation: Gretchen's Caesar breakdown is a brilliant piece of sustained joke construction. The gradual erosion of academic language into naked personal grievance is perfectly escalated — 'just as cute,' 'people totally like,' 'when did it become OK for one person to be the boss of everybody' — until it tips into 'we should totally just stab Caesar!' The word 'totally' doing double duty (teen idiom and academic analysis) is a great comic choice. Character integration is exceptional: only Gretchen, whose entire identity is suppressing resentment of Regina, could have this breakdown in this way. High rewatch bonus because it's even funnier knowing what comes before it.

jokes.text: You know that I'm not allowed to wear hoop earrings, right? Yeah. Two years ago, she told me that hoop earrings were HER thing and that I wasn't allowed to wear them anymore.
jokes.setup: Gretchen has cracked and is revealing Regina's abuses
jokes.punchline: The first specific example of Regina's tyranny is that she banned Gretchen from wearing a type of earring — 'her thing' — and Gretchen has complied for two years
jokes.explanation: The specific absurdity of hoop earrings being 'claimed' as someone's thing — and Gretchen accepting that claim for two years — is very good social satire. The escalation of the story (expensive Hanukkah gift she had to pretend not to like) makes it funnier and sadder. Good cringe comedy.

jokes.text: And you know she cheats on Aaron? Every Thursday he thinks she's doing SAT prep. But really, she's hooking up with Shane Oman in the projection room above the auditorium. And I never told anybody that because... I'm such a good friend.
jokes.setup: Gretchen continues her confessional breakdown of Regina's secrets
jokes.punchline: After revealing the most damaging secret yet (affair, specific details), Gretchen concludes with '...I'm such a good friend' — the total inversion of what she's just done, delivered with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: The punchline 'I'm such a good friend' after spilling the most damaging secret imaginable is perfect ironic self-delusion. The beat before it — the ellipsis, the pause before she delivers the self-assessment — is crucial. It lands because Gretchen genuinely believes it. Very high character integration: this is exactly how someone in Gretchen's psychological position (loyalty and resentment in equal measure) would speak. The specificity of 'SAT prep on Thursdays / projection room above the auditorium' is also good — it has the texture of real knowledge.

jokes.text: My purse! / Looks like he's headed for the projection room above the auditorium!
jokes.setup: Janis and Damian try to orchestrate Aaron catching Regina cheating; they apparently cause or witness a distraction with someone (presumably Shane Oman) dropping a purse
jokes.punchline: Damian's overly theatrical announcement of the target's direction — 'looks like he's headed for the projection room above the auditorium!' — delivered as if narrating a nature documentary or police stakeout
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'projection room above the auditorium' (now a repeated phrase with its own rhythm) is funny because of its specificity. Damian's dramatic delivery of a mundane direction is a character beat. The plan-falling-apart montage is light physical comedy.

jokes.text: Aaron is about to catch Regina and Shane Oman — Cady's voiceover: 'Looks like he's headed for the projection room above the auditorium!'
jokes.setup: Cady and her co-conspirators have spent weeks trying to engineer Aaron catching Regina cheating.
jokes.punchline: The sports-commentary delivery of 'He's headed for the projection room!' — treating a teenage love-triangle stakeout like a live sporting event.
jokes.explanation: Good running commentary joke. The gap between the high drama of the voiceover and the mundane reality is funny. The specificity of 'projection room above the auditorium' (echoing Gretchen's revelation verbatim) is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Coach Carr? Trang Pak? / Guys, why did we think we could do this? We're amateurs.
jokes.setup: In the projection room, they discover it's not Shane Oman with Regina — it's the school health teacher Coach Carr with a student named Trang Pak
jokes.punchline: The discovery of a teacher-student affair (much worse than what they were looking for) causes them to give up and declare themselves 'amateurs' — as if the lesson is they were outclassed by the scandal level
jokes.explanation: Dark subversive gag — the punchline is discovering something far more scandalous than what they set out to find, and their response is to feel outclassed rather than horrified. 'We're amateurs' perfectly captures the absurdist logic: the scandal is so out of their league they should concede the field. Good economy and a surprising turn.

jokes.text: What are Kälteen bars? / They're these weird Swedish nutrition bars. My mom used to give them to the kids in Africa to help them gain weight. / They're these weird nutrition bars my mom uses to lose weight. / Give me it.
jokes.setup: Cady presents Kälteen bars as diet bars to Regina (who wants to lose weight); the audience learns from Cady's voiceover that they are actually weight-gain bars
jokes.punchline: Cady's explanation to Janis/Damian ('gain weight') is juxtaposed against her lie to Regina ('lose weight'), then Regina immediately demands one — the speed of her trust and greed is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The two-track explanation — truth to Janis/Damian, lie to Regina — is structurally clean and maximally efficient. The irony of Regina eagerly accepting what will make her gain weight (what she fears most) is a satisfying dark comedy setup. 'Give me it' as the trigger is perfectly impulsive. Excellent economy; the audience gets both the setup and the trap in about 10 seconds.

jokes.text: It burns carbs. It just burns up all your carbs. / I really wanna lose 3 pounds.
jokes.setup: Cady elaborates on the fake weight-loss properties of Kälteen bars; Regina can't identify the secret ingredient
jokes.punchline: Regina's response to any health/weight claim is always the same: 'I really wanna lose 3 pounds' — the callback to her established refrain lands as a running gag while also underlining the trap Cady has set
jokes.explanation: 'I really wanna lose 3 pounds' has become a Pavlovian response for Regina whenever body/weight is mentioned. Its third(ish) occurrence in the film has diminishing marginal surprise but increasing contextual irony — she's about to gain weight eating these bars, not lose 3 pounds. The callback mechanism is working.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, what are you talking about? You're so skinny. / Shut up.
jokes.setup: Cady protests Regina's body anxiety as a manipulation tactic
jokes.punchline: Regina's 'Shut up' in response to a sincere compliment about her body — she doesn't want to be told she doesn't need to lose weight, she wants to lose weight — is a perfect character beat that also reveals Cady's fakery is working
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat — Regina can't accept compliments because they undermine her self-image. Functional but not remarkable.

jokes.text: She knew it was better to be in The Plastics, hating life, than to not be in at all.
jokes.setup: Cady observes how Gretchen keeps coming back to Regina despite the abuse
jokes.punchline: The blunt formulation 'hating life' as the state of being in The Plastics — delivered as a neutral observation — is funny because of its frankness and because it's exactly right
jokes.explanation: Fey's social satire in compact form — 'hating life' as the standard condition of popularity. It's a sharp observational line that lands with wry recognition.

jokes.text: That new girl moved here from Africa. / I saw Cady Heron wearing Army pants and flip-flops, so I bought Army pants and flip-flops. / That Cady girl is hot. She might even be hotter than Regina George.
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover explains that being with The Plastics means being famous and having people know things about you
jokes.punchline: The 'things people know' escalate from factual (Africa) to absurd-mimicry (buying Army pants and flip-flops because Cady wore them) to provocative social threat (hotter than Regina George)
jokes.explanation: The 'Army pants and flip-flops' line became a cultural reference — the idea that one sighting of a popular girl in an outfit triggers mass mimicry is a great satire of teenage conformity. The escalation from information to behavior to social threat is well-structured. 'I saw Cady Heron wearing Army pants and flip-flops, so I bought Army pants and flip-flops' is the best individual beat and extremely quotable.

jokes.text: I spent about 80 percent of my time talking about Regina. And the other 20 percent of the time, I was praying for someone else to bring her up so I could talk about her more.
jokes.setup: Cady narrates that she was obsessed with Regina
jokes.punchline: The 20% she WASN'T talking about Regina was spent hoping someone else would bring her up — total self-awareness of her own obsession
jokes.explanation: The mathematical framing of obsession is sharp and self-aware. The structure is clean: the first percentage sets up a mild confession, the second percentage escalates it into something more pathetic and funnier. Good economy and character specificity — it's a Cady joke that couldn't belong to a less self-aware narrator.

jokes.text: She's not even that good-looking if you really look at her. I don't know. Now that she's getting fatter, she's got pretty big jugs.
jokes.setup: Cady is trying to tear Regina down
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to insult Regina accidentally becomes a compliment ('pretty big jugs'), revealing how deep in her own head she is
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Cady's own obsession undermines her attempt at dismissal — she can't even properly insult Regina without noting something appealing. The comedic irony is well-structured and character-specific.

jokes.text: I have this theory that if you cut all her hair off, she'd look like a British man. / Yeah, I know. You told me that one before.
jokes.setup: Cady shares yet another anti-Regina theory
jokes.punchline: The listener has already heard it — Cady is so obsessed she's recycling material without noticing
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. The specific absurdity of the theory ('look like a British man') is funny on its own, but the deflating callback — 'you told me that one before' — doubles it by confirming Cady's obsession has reached delusional repetition. Two laughs in two lines.

jokes.text: You smell like a baby prostitute.
jokes.setup: Cady mentions Regina gave her perfume
jokes.punchline: Janis's blunt, specific, and deeply weird assessment: 'baby prostitute'
jokes.explanation: Three words that have become one of the most quoted lines in the entire film. The juxtaposition of 'baby' (innocent) and 'prostitute' (transgressive) is maximally compressed and specific. Janis's deadpan delivery would amplify it. It's also character-perfect: exactly the kind of acerbic, transgressive thing Janis would say. Economy is essentially perfect — 10. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it in cultural impact.

jokes.text: Damn, Africa, what happened? (after seeing Cady's low math score)
jokes.setup: Aaron sees Cady got a low score on a math test
jokes.punchline: 'Damn, Africa, what happened?' — referencing her African origin as an explanation for why she should be better at math (ironic reversal of usual stereotype assumptions)
jokes.explanation: The nickname 'Africa' is a callback to earlier reels establishing Cady's backstory. The line is punchy and quotable. The humor comes from Aaron's breezy assumption that an African kid should excel at math — a gentle satirical jab at American cluelessness. It's well-known from the film but not among the most sophisticated constructions.

jokes.text: Well, the first time I did it, I got a zero. / Wrong. / But then when I checked it, I got... / ...one. / There you go.
jokes.setup: Cady is pretending to need tutoring in math
jokes.punchline: She 'improves' from zero to one — Aaron enthusiastically validates this microscopic improvement, oblivious to how bad it is
jokes.explanation: The joke rewards the audience that understands Cady is deliberately sandbagging. Aaron's earnest 'There you go' is funny precisely because he's oblivious to the ruse. Gets better on rewatch when you know the full scheme.

jokes.text: Man, look, I... I can't do this. (Aaron stops fake-tutoring and confesses his conflict)
jokes.setup: The tutoring session is going well and Cady is gaining ground with Aaron
jokes.punchline: Aaron suddenly breaks the mood with sudden moral crisis — the audience knows this is ALL fake on Cady's side, amplifying the irony
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat with comedic irony underpinning it. The humor is situational — the audience knows Cady is manipulating him — but Aaron's sincere guilt isn't itself a strong joke.

jokes.text: She's cheating on you! (Cady blurts out word vomit to Aaron)
jokes.setup: Cady describes 'word vomit' — things she says before she can stop herself. Aaron is expressing loyalty to Regina.
jokes.punchline: Despite being part of the scheme to destroy Regina, the impulsive blurt comes out anyway — she can't control herself
jokes.explanation: First deployment of the 'word vomit' running gag as a plot device. The setup is well-prepared and the payoff is structurally satisfying. The irony — she's executing a plan but also acting impulsively — is nicely layered.

jokes.text: I gave him everything. I was half a virgin when I met him.
jokes.setup: Regina is devastated that Aaron found out she was cheating
jokes.punchline: 'Half a virgin' — a logically nonsensical claim delivered with complete earnestness by Regina
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. 'Half a virgin' is an oxymoron that Regina deploys with total sincerity, as though it's a coherent defense of her virtue. Only Regina George could say this — it perfectly captures her narcissistic logic and her complete detachment from how language works. Highly quotable. Character integration is exceptional.

jokes.text: You wanna do something fun? You wanna go to Taco Bell? / I can't go to Taco Bell, I'm on an all-carb diet.
jokes.setup: Regina is upset; Karen tries to cheer her up with Taco Bell
jokes.punchline: Regina says she can't go because she's 'on an all-carb diet' — which is the OPPOSITE of a diet
jokes.explanation: Brilliant in context because we've already been told Cady is feeding Regina Kälteen bars to make her gain weight, and now Regina is simultaneously going on an 'all-carb diet' (incoherent) and refusing Taco Bell. The joke works on two levels: Regina's confused reasoning and the dramatic irony of her sabotage.

jokes.text: God, Karen, you are so stupid!
jokes.setup: Karen suggests Taco Bell as emotional support
jokes.punchline: Regina's explosive, disproportionate response to a sincere suggestion
jokes.explanation: Classic Regina cruelty, but fairly stock. What elevates it slightly is Karen's genuine attempt to help, making the explosion funnier. Character-appropriate but not Fey's most inventive line.

jokes.text: I can put my whole fist in my mouth. Wanna see?
jokes.setup: Cady asks Karen what she's good at, trying to find something to validate her
jokes.punchline: Karen's proudest skill is putting her entire fist in her mouth — offered earnestly
jokes.explanation: Perfect Karen joke. The setup (name something you're good at) creates an expectation of a human, relatable answer. Karen delivers something completely unhinged yet sincere. The 'Wanna see?' makes it worse (better). Pure character comedy at its finest — this joke could ONLY be Karen.

jokes.text: I'm kind of psychic. I have a fifth sense.
jokes.setup: Cady asks if Karen has any other talents
jokes.punchline: Karen claims psychic powers but calls it a 'fifth sense' instead of 'sixth sense' — not knowing there are only five
jokes.explanation: Karen saying 'fifth sense' is a perfect crystallization of her character — she's not dumb enough to know she's being dumb. The reference to 'The Sixth Sense' is implicit and adds a layer. 'It's like I have ESPN or something' follows immediately as an even better punchline. High quotability.

jokes.text: It's like I have ESPN or something.
jokes.setup: Karen has just claimed she has a 'fifth sense' (psychic ability)
jokes.punchline: She illustrates it by confusing ESPN (a sports network) with ESP (extrasensory perception)
jokes.explanation: One of the great dumb-character jokes in modern comedy. The confusion of ESPN with ESP is specific, surprising, and perfect. It couldn't be more economical — four words. It's character-defining: Karen isn't just dumb, she's dumb in this exact, particular way. Genuinely in the tier of 8.0+ anchor jokes and arguably iconic. The 'fifth sense' setup makes it even better — we think we have the joke, then she deepens it.

jokes.text: My breasts can always tell when it's gonna rain.
jokes.setup: Karen claims psychic ability via 'ESPN'
jokes.punchline: Her psychic power manifests as her breasts predicting rain — an absurdist, calmly stated claim
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the Karen psychic bit. The jump from vague psychic claims to 'my breasts can tell when it's raining' is absurdist and deeply character-specific. Pure Karen. The delivery would be completely earnest, making it funnier. Among the most quotable lines in the film.

jokes.text: Really? That's amazing. / Well, they can tell when it's raining.
jokes.setup: Karen claims her breasts can tell when it's going to rain
jokes.punchline: Cady's straight-man 'Really? That's amazing' is immediately deflated: Karen corrects herself — they can only tell when it's ALREADY raining
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the Karen psychic sequence. Cady's sincere compliment sets up an expectation that Karen's power is real, and then Karen's self-correction — 'well, they can tell when it's raining' (i.e., the most useless possible form of this power) — is a masterclass in comedic deflation. Perfect structure: build, validate, collapse. The callback to 'raining vs. gonna rain' distinction is devastatingly efficient. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor; this edges above it in structural perfection.

jokes.text: Do you guys need anything? Some snacks? A condom? Let me know. Oh, God love you.
jokes.setup: Regina's mom pops in to check on Regina and her new boyfriend
jokes.punchline: She offers 'a condom' in the same breath as 'snacks' — cheerfully encouraging her teenage daughter's sex life
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'Some snacks? A condom?' — the juxtaposition of domestic hospitality with sexual facilitation — perfectly defines the George household dynamic. 'Oh, God love you' as a kicker cements Regina's mom as a vivid, specific comedic character. Well-structured and character-specific.

jokes.text: Aaron had dumped Regina, and she was unknowingly eating 5,000 calories a day.
jokes.setup: Cady narrates the status of her scheme
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, matter-of-fact narration of deliberately fattening someone is darkly funny — framed like a progress report
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the gap between Cady's breezy tone and the actual malevolence of what she's doing. Effective but not exceptional — the punchline is implicit rather than explicit.

jokes.text: Janis Ian nominated for Spring Fling Queen — 'What is happening to the world?'
jokes.setup: Spring Fling Queen nominees are being announced in an evidently popularity-based selection
jokes.punchline: Janis Ian — the school's resident art-punk outcast — is announced as a nominee, prompting Damian's incredulous reaction
jokes.explanation: Good situational comedy — the juxtaposition of Janis Ian with 'Spring Fling Queen' is inherently funny. Damian's reaction line is sharp. The setup (Plastics being nominated) makes the left-field inclusion funnier.

jokes.text: Damian, you put me in there too? That's not part of the plan. / I didn't put you in there. / You mean I'm really nominated?
jokes.setup: Cady is surprised to hear her name called as a Spring Fling nominee
jokes.punchline: She assumes Damian manipulated it — but it was real — revealing that she's inadvertently become popular enough to earn a genuine nomination
jokes.explanation: Nice structural beat — Cady's default assumption that it must be a manipulation reveals how thoroughly she's adopted the Plastic mindset. The comedic irony is well-executed.

jokes.text: It won't close. / It's a 5. / OK, it must be marked wrong.
jokes.setup: Regina tries on a dress she put on hold — which now doesn't fit because of the Kälteen bar sabotage
jokes.punchline: Regina immediately concludes the dress is 'marked wrong' rather than that she's gained weight — perfect narcissistic denial
jokes.explanation: The joke rewards those tracking the Kälteen bar plot. Regina's narcissism — she couldn't possibly have gained weight, the dress must be wrong — is a perfect character beat. The deadpan certainty of 'it must be marked wrong' is excellent.

jokes.text: You know Swedish? / Yeah, everyone in Africa can read Swedish.
jokes.setup: Cady explains the Kälteen bars using their (fictitious) Swedish label
jokes.punchline: Regina asks if Cady speaks Swedish; Cady sarcastically responds that all Africans read Swedish — a ridiculous claim delivered with deadpan confidence
jokes.explanation: Brilliant satirical jab at the American stereotype of Africa as a monolith. Cady weaponizes Regina's ignorance against her — Regina accepts the absurd claim because she doesn't know enough to question it. The structure is perfect: a reasonable question, an insane answer, delivered straight. Highly quotable and sharp on multiple levels.

jokes.text: Sorry. We only carry sizes 1, 3 and 5. You could try Sears.
jokes.setup: Regina asks if the dress comes in the next size up
jokes.punchline: 'You could try Sears' — the deadpan nuclear option, suggesting Regina shop at a discount department store
jokes.explanation: The store name '1-3-5' (carrying only odd small sizes) is itself a sharp satirical detail, but the punchline 'You could try Sears' is the gem. For a Plastic, being directed to Sears is a social death sentence. The salesgirl delivers it with no apparent malice, which makes it land harder. Economy is near-perfect: six words do enormous comedic damage.

jokes.text: You know what's weird about your quizzes, Cady, is that all the work is right and just the answers are wrong.
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury calls Cady in because she's failing math
jokes.punchline: The teacher has noticed the tell-tale sign of deliberate failure — all the work is correct, only the answers are wrong
jokes.explanation: Sharp structural observation that makes Cady's scheme feel freshly absurd — she's so mathematically gifted that even her deliberate failures are logically consistent. The audience has known the scheme; Ms. Norbury figuring it out from the evidence is satisfying and funny.

jokes.text: I'm divorced. I'm broke from getting divorced. The only guy that ever calls my house is Randy from Chase Visa.
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury is advising Cady not to dumb herself down for boys; Cady asks 'How would you know?'
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury launches into a cascade of personal humiliations — divorced, broke, only gets calls from a debt collector named Randy
jokes.explanation: Tina Fey writing for her own character — Ms. Norbury's self-deprecating overshare is perfectly calibrated. 'Randy from Chase Visa' is a specifically named detail that elevates it from generic to real. The cascade structure (divorced → broke from divorce → Randy) escalates nicely.

jokes.text: Because I'm a pusher. I push people. I pushed my husband into law school. That was a bust.
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury explains her philosophy of pushing people to succeed
jokes.punchline: 'I pushed my husband into law school. That was a bust.' — the casual aside reveals her entire backstory in five words
jokes.explanation: Classic Tina Fey economy. 'That was a bust' appended to 'I pushed my husband into law school' implies an entire failed marriage and professional resentment in four words. The understatement of 'a bust' is perfect — no over-explanation, no milking. This is how great comedy writers handle exposition.

jokes.text: I hate her! I mean, she's totally failing me on purpose because I didn't join those stupid Mathletes! She was so queer. She was like, 'I'm a pusher, Cady. I'm a pusher.' What does that even mean? / Like a drug pusher? / Probably.
jokes.setup: Cady tells the Plastics about Ms. Norbury's speech; they mock her
jokes.punchline: Regina genuinely theorizes that Ms. Norbury is a drug dealer — the trio's collective stupidity/cruelty produces this absurd conclusion
jokes.explanation: The callback works beautifully: Fey writes herself a speech about pushing people, then has the Plastics misread it as drug dealing, which will pay off later when Cady actually writes this in the Burn Book. The 'probably' is the killer punchline — delivered with Plastic-girl casual certainty.

jokes.text: You let it out, honey. Put it in the book.
jokes.setup: Cady is venting about Ms. Norbury to the Plastics
jokes.punchline: Gretchen encourages Cady to write the slander in the Burn Book — framed as emotional support/therapy
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the therapeutic framing of a genuinely awful act. 'You let it out, honey' sounds like supportive friendship; 'put it in the book' reveals it's vicious. Effective dark comedy.

jokes.text: I know it may look like I'd become a bitch, but that's only because I was acting like a bitch.
jokes.setup: Cady's voiceover addresses the audience directly about her transformation
jokes.punchline: The 'distinction' she offers — 'that's only because I was acting like a bitch' — is no distinction at all, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest meta-satirical lines in the film. Tina Fey has Cady make a distinction that isn't a distinction — a logical tautology delivered as though it's a meaningful clarification. It's both a character reveal (Cady's self-delusion) and a meta-commentary on how we rationalize bad behavior. High quotability, great economy.

jokes.text: Oh, I planned this one on my own. Love you. Bye.
jokes.setup: Janis confronts Cady about why she can't come to her art show or hang out
jokes.punchline: Cady accidentally reveals she's ditching Janis for a solo Plastic scheme, then blithely says 'Love you. Bye.' — the affection completely at odds with what she just said
jokes.explanation: The casual 'Love you. Bye.' as a dismissal after a hurtful revelation is a character beat more than a standalone joke. Works in context as a measure of Cady's transformation.

jokes.text: The three-way phone call sequence — Cady masterminds Gretchen and Regina insulting each other while each thinks Cady is on their side
jokes.setup: Cady is manipulating both Gretchen and Regina via three-way phone call without their knowledge
jokes.punchline: The complexity escalates as each party says something terrible about the other, with Cady facilitating — a masterclass in escalating dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: The three-way call sequence is a structurally brilliant sustained comedy bit. It's not built on individual punchlines but on escalating situational irony — each line is funnier because we know what the others don't. The 'hold on' repetition works as a running rhythm. Scores well on structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, she's so annoying. / I know. Just get rid of her.
jokes.setup: Regina is on one line complaining about Gretchen; Cady is simultaneously on the other line with Gretchen
jokes.punchline: Regina and Cady bond over how annoying Gretchen is — while Gretchen is on hold on the other line
jokes.explanation: Part of the three-way call sequence. The simultaneous betrayal of Gretchen by both Regina AND Cady — with Gretchen on hold — is a sharp comedic irony. Functions well within the sustained bit.

jokes.text: Regina says everyone hates you because you're such a slut. / She said that? / You didn't hear it from me. / Little harsh, Gretch. / Whatever. She has a right to know.
jokes.setup: Three-way call; Cady relays Regina's words to Gretchen
jokes.punchline: Karen's 'Little harsh, Gretch' — moral concern from Karen is funny given her own casual cruelty — and Gretchen's 'she has a right to know' self-justification
jokes.explanation: Karen showing a flash of moral concern ('little harsh') is funny because it's such a low bar and because Karen is not known for her moral acuity. The payoff on Gretchen's self-justification adds another beat.

jokes.text: I can't go out. I'm sick. / Boo. You whore.
jokes.setup: Karen begs off with an excuse
jokes.punchline: Regina's response to Karen saying she's sick: 'Boo. You whore.' — casual cruelty compressed into three words
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the entire film. 'Boo. You whore.' — the full stop between 'Boo' and 'You whore' is essential to the joke. It's perfectly compressed: casual disappointment followed by a disproportionate insult, delivered as though both are of equal weight. Only Regina George says this. Economy is as close to perfect as dialogue gets.

jokes.text: Is butter a carb?
jokes.setup: Cady and friends are about to have a serious confrontation with Regina about breaking the dress code
jokes.punchline: Regina responds to the gravity of the situation by asking if butter is a carb — Kälteen bar obsession has addled her thinking
jokes.explanation: Among the most iconic lines in the film. The juxtaposition of a heavy dramatic confrontation with Regina's airheaded diet question is a brilliant non-sequitur. Only Regina would redirect a moment of social reckoning to a nutrition question. Maximum economy — four words. It has become a cultural touchstone. Comparable to the highest-tier anchor jokes.

jokes.text: Regina, you're wearing sweatpants. It's Monday. / So? / So that's against the rules, and you can't sit with us.
jokes.setup: Gretchen and Karen enforce the Plastics' dress code against Regina herself
jokes.punchline: The rules Regina created are now being applied to her — the dictator deposed by her own laws
jokes.explanation: The satisfying structural irony of Regina being expelled by her own rules is sharp plotting-as-comedy. 'You can't sit with us' becomes immediately iconic as it's deployed against its own originator. The setup (her rules, her table) makes the punchline earned and structurally elegant.

jokes.text: They were real that day I wore a vest. / Because that vest was disgusting.
jokes.setup: Regina argues the dress-code rules aren't real
jokes.punchline: Gretchen reveals she enforced the vest rule because the vest was actually disgusting — confirming the rules ARE real and always have been weaponizable
jokes.explanation: The 'vest' detail is a great example of Fey's specificity. It implies a whole backstory of Gretchen being silently judged for her vest while pretending to agree with the rules. A sharp, quick backstory joke.

jokes.text: These sweatpants are all that fits me right now.
jokes.setup: Regina is being expelled from her own table for wearing sweatpants
jokes.punchline: Regina's pathetic admission that she can only fit into sweatpants — paying off the Kälteen bar plot with maximum humiliation
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Kälteen bar plot is delivered in this single, devastating sentence. Regina's transformation from queen to someone whose only fitting clothes are sweatpants is both funny and unexpectedly poignant. High quotability. The simplicity of the admission makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Watch where you're going, fat-ass!
jokes.setup: Regina storms out of the cafeteria and apparently gets hit by a school bus (or narrowly avoids one)
jokes.punchline: The driver (or someone) yells 'fat-ass' at the queen bee who just had her status publicly destroyed — the indignity continues to pile on
jokes.explanation: A broad escalation beat — the insult adds to Regina's humiliation cascade but doesn't have sophisticated craft behind it. Works in context as a cap to the cafeteria sequence.

jokes.text: Gretchen and Karen followed me around all afternoon. 'So, what are we doing this weekend?' 'Yeah, what are we doing?'
jokes.setup: Regina has just been toppled; Gretchen and Karen immediately transfer their loyalty to Cady
jokes.punchline: Their instant switch — asking Cady what 'we' are doing — perfectly parodies the vacuum of Plastic loyalty
jokes.explanation: The instant transfer of Plastic allegiance satirizes social hierarchies sharply — these girls have no actual loyalty, only strategic attachment. The echoing 'Yeah, what are we doing?' from Karen is perfect.

jokes.text: We have tickets for this thing. / What? / What? / Was I the new queen bee? / I can try and get out of it. / Yeah. / Yeah. / Because I told my friend Janis I'd go to her art show. / We've had these tickets for months. / You love Ladysmith Black Mambazo.
jokes.setup: Cady tests her new queen bee status by announcing she needs to ditch a commitment
jokes.punchline: Even her parents capitulate to her new authority — 'You love Ladysmith Black Mambazo' is a desperate parental plea — while Gretchen and Karen echo her choices reflexively
jokes.explanation: 'You love Ladysmith Black Mambazo' is a great specific detail — the incongruously specific band name as a parental argument is funny in its particularity. The scene works as an escalating confirmation that Cady has assumed full Plastic power.

jokes.text: Hey. I'm having a small get-together at my house tomorrow night. / Is Regina going? / No. Do you think I'm an idiot? / No, it's just gonna be a few cool people, and you better be one of them, byotch.
jokes.setup: Cady invites Aaron to a party
jokes.punchline: Aaron's first question is about Regina — revealing the shadow she still casts — and Cady's 'byotch' is a funny self-conscious attempt at cool casualness
jokes.explanation: Light character comedy. 'Byotch' as Cady's attempt at Plastic cool is an effective character moment but not a strong standalone joke. Gets a chuckle but nothing more.

jokes.text: Aaron Samuels was going to be in my touse at my party.
jokes.setup: Cady is narrating her excitement about the party
jokes.punchline: 'Touse' — Cady mispronounces 'house' in her narration, a small signal of her character's occasional foreignness
jokes.explanation: A subtle character-comedy beat — 'touse' is a mild mispronunciation that reminds us of Cady's outsider status. Small laugh, minor craft.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. / You look awesome! / You look awesome! / I know, right?
jokes.setup: Cady is anxious about looking perfect for her party; asks her friends if she looks good
jokes.punchline: Both friends simultaneously give effusive compliments; Cady responds 'I know, right?' — having fully absorbed Plastic self-confidence
jokes.explanation: Light character-transformation joke. 'I know, right?' shows Cady's Regina-ification. Not especially inventive but functional.

jokes.text: It was not enough. Somehow, the word had gotten out about my small get-together.
jokes.setup: Cady planned a small gathering for eight people and carefully prepared snacks for eight
jokes.punchline: The party has clearly exploded — the precise preparation for eight people collides with an apparently massive crowd
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom party-spiraling setup. The gag of 'cheese and crackers for eight' being woefully insufficient is familiar but Cady's genuine surprise is charming. Functional.

jokes.text: Dude, put on 'The Ramayana Monkey Chant'.
jokes.setup: Random party chaos — someone is at the music
jokes.punchline: The request for the Ramayana Monkey Chant at a high school party is a brilliantly specific absurdist detail — it's exactly the kind of thing a tryhard would request
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Ramayana Monkey Chant' as a party music request is funny precisely because of how unexpected and odd it is. Good absurdist detail from Fey.

jokes.text: She thinks she's gonna have a party and not invite me? Who does she think she is? I, like, invented her, you know what I mean?
jokes.setup: Regina shows up at Cady's party uninvited
jokes.punchline: 'I invented her' — Regina takes credit for creating Cady, oblivious to the fact that Cady is the one dismantling her
jokes.explanation: Perfect Regina narcissism. She's simultaneously right (she did introduce Cady to Plastic life) and catastrophically wrong (Cady is using that access to destroy her). The irony is sharp and character-specific.

jokes.text: Look, I don't wanna hurt your feelings, but I only date women of color.
jokes.setup: Gretchen approaches a guy at the party romantically
jokes.punchline: The guy's rejection of Gretchen is delivered with exaggerated politeness but with a comically specific, outlandish reason — 'I only date women of color'
jokes.explanation: The formal politeness of 'I don't want to hurt your feelings, but...' followed by a very specific exclusionary preference is funny for its bluntness. The specificity of the reason makes it funnier than a generic rejection.

jokes.text: You look... / New clothes? / Thanks.
jokes.setup: Aaron and Cady finally find each other at the party; Aaron is clearly about to compliment her
jokes.punchline: He loses his train of thought and pivots to 'New clothes?' — an awkward deflation of a romantic moment
jokes.explanation: Light cringe comedy — the deflated compliment is a believable teenage awkwardness beat. Functional but not notable.

jokes.text: I pretended to be bad at math so that you'd help me. But the thing is, I'm not really bad at math. I'm actually really good at math. You're kind of bad at math. Anyways, now I'm failing. Isn't that funny?
jokes.setup: Cady decides to confess her scheme to Aaron, expecting him to find it charming
jokes.punchline: She confidently reveals her manipulation, then tells him he's 'kind of bad at math,' and ends with 'Isn't that funny?' — completely misreading how this will land
jokes.explanation: The progression of this confession is perfectly written. Each sentence that Cady thinks makes it better actually makes it worse — 'you're kind of bad at math' is a gratuitous additional insult she doesn't even realize she's delivering. 'Isn't that funny?' is the peak of comedic obliviousness. Character comedy at its best.

jokes.text: So why didn't you just talk to me? / Well, because I couldn't. Because of Regina. Because you were her property... / Her property?
jokes.setup: Aaron asks why Cady didn't just approach him instead of the math scheme.
jokes.punchline: Cady accidentally calls him Regina's 'property' — a word that hits Aaron like an insult and is funnier for being accidentally accurate.
jokes.explanation: Good beat — 'property' is both accidentally honest and a slip that torpedoes the conversation. Aaron's reaction ('Her property?') is funny because it's both offended and slightly accurate. The escalation into their argument is well-structured.

jokes.text: What is this?! / Actual vomit.
jokes.setup: Cady has been talking about 'word vomit' throughout the film; during the disastrous party confession she actually vomits on Aaron
jokes.punchline: The 'word vomit' metaphor pays off literally — Cady vomits for real. 'Actual vomit' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: The best structurally-constructed joke in this reel and among the best in the film. The 'word vomit' metaphor has been carefully planted and deployed twice already; paying it off with literal vomit is both a perfect running-gag resolution and a physical comedy escalation. 'Actual vomit' as the button is two words that earn massive laughs because of everything that came before. This is elite comedy construction — it rewards attention, pays off a setup that spans the whole act, and has a physical comedy escalation that feels earned rather than cheap. Comparable to the top anchor examples.

jokes.text: Oh, God. You dirty little liar. / I'm sorry. I can explain. / Explain how you forgot to invite us to your party?
jokes.setup: Cady braces for Janis to call her out for the manipulation/betrayal
jokes.punchline: Janis's big accusation is about not being invited to the party — a deliberately shallow grievance after everything Cady has done
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is structurally nice — the audience expects the big moral confrontation, but Janis deflates it into a petty complaint about the party invite. This undercuts the drama with comedy effectively.

jokes.text: Did you have an awesome time? Did you drink awesome shooters and listen to awesome music, and then just sit around and soak up each other's awesomeness?
jokes.setup: Janis and Damian confront Cady outside the party for not inviting them.
jokes.punchline: Janis's withering sarcasm — the triple 'awesome' escalating to 'soak up each other's awesomeness' — is both funny and devastating. It's a perfect skewering of Plastic culture.
jokes.explanation: One of Janis's best lines. The escalating 'awesome' repetition builds perfectly — it starts sarcastic and ends dripping with contempt. 'Soak up each other's awesomeness' is the perfect final note. Very quotable and deeply character-specific to Janis's satirical voice.

jokes.text: Oh, I used to live in Africa with all the little birdies and the little monkeys.
jokes.setup: Janis is mocking Cady's self-presentation as the innocent African newcomer
jokes.punchline: Janis does a mock-innocent voice caricaturing how Cady sold herself — 'little birdies and the little monkeys' is a deliberately infantilizing distortion
jokes.explanation: Janis's mimicry of Cady's Africa backstory as naive and self-serving is a sharp satirical jab at how 'exotic' backgrounds get used as social currency. The 'little birdies and the little monkeys' exaggeration is funny in its precise cruelty.

jokes.text: It's not my fault you're in love with me or something! / What?! / Oh, no she did not!
jokes.setup: Cady and Janis are in a heated argument
jokes.punchline: Cady lobs an accusation of romantic feelings at Janis; Damian's 'Oh, no she did not!' is the perfect Greek-chorus reaction
jokes.explanation: Damian's reaction steals this moment — his 'Oh, no she did not!' is a perfect audience-surrogate response. The accusation itself is funny in its desperation (Cady weaponizing a Plastic-girl move in a genuine argument), and Damian's horror elevates it.

jokes.text: Like Aaron Samuels, for example. He broke up with Regina and guess what. He still doesn't want you.
jokes.setup: Janis is delivering her full indictment of Cady
jokes.punchline: The aside about Aaron — delivered as evidence of Cady's delusion — is a cold, cutting observation that's funny in its brutal specificity
jokes.explanation: The 'and guess what — he still doesn't want you' is a sharply economical line. It redirects the whole argument to demonstrate that Cady's schemes haven't even achieved her actual goal. Janis is at her most cutting here.

jokes.text: Here. You can have this. It won a prize.
jokes.setup: Janis ends her confrontation with Cady at the party
jokes.punchline: She hands Cady her award-winning art — the ultimate passive-aggressive parting gift that highlights everything Cady missed
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the art show callbacks — Janis went, it won a prize, and Cady missed it — is delivered with withering economy. 'It won a prize' as the kicker is quietly devastating.

jokes.text: And I want my pink shirt back! / I want my pink shirt back!
jokes.setup: Damian has been wanting his pink shirt back from Cady throughout the film (established in earlier reels)
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a dramatic confrontation, Damian inserts his mundane demand — twice — for the pink shirt
jokes.explanation: Damian derailing a climactic moment of genuine emotional confrontation with his highly personal grievance about the pink shirt is perfectly timed comedy relief. The repetition (he says it twice) escalates the absurdity. 'I want my pink shirt back!' has become one of the film's signature lines. Pure character comedy.

jokes.text: It's like I can't trust anyone anymore.
jokes.setup: Cady is upset after the confrontation with Janis
jokes.punchline: Cady complaining she can't trust anyone — after she spent the entire reel deceiving and manipulating everyone around her
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony — the character is entirely unaware that she is the least trustworthy person in the room. Good but straightforward situational irony.

jokes.text: Why are you eating a Kälteen bar? / I'm starving. / Man, I hate those things. Coach Carr makes us eat those when we wanna move up a weight class.
jokes.setup: Cady sees Regina still eating a Kälteen bar despite everything falling apart
jokes.punchline: A football player reveals Kälteen bars are used by athletes to GAIN weight — Cady's sabotage is exposed in the most offhand way possible
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural comedy: the most elaborate scheme in the film is undone by a random football player casually mentioning what the bars are actually for. The timing (immediately after Cady has lost everything else) is excellent. The irony that Regina is STILL eating them even as the truth emerges is a great beat. Well-constructed reveal that closes the Kälteen arc with maximum economy.

jokes.text: Mother... (Cady realizes her scheme has backfired)
jokes.setup: Cady learns the Kälteen bars make you GAIN weight — her sabotage has been real all along
jokes.punchline: The truncated expletive 'Mother...' — the barely-restrained curse is funnier than any full word
jokes.explanation: The cut-off swear is a classic comedic device but executed with perfect timing here. The audience can complete it themselves, which makes it funnier. Economy essentially perfect.

jokes.text: This girl is the nastiest skank bitch I've ever met. Do not trust her. She is a fugly slut!
jokes.setup: The Burn Book pages begin circulating — the first page we see is the entry about someone (the audience realizes it's written about various girls)
jokes.punchline: The escalating insults — 'nastiest skank bitch,' 'fugly slut' — delivered in formal dramatic narration, are darkly funny in their viciousness
jokes.explanation: The Burn Book content is funny primarily through accumulation and escalation. The individual entries are blunt-force instruments rather than crafted jokes, but the deployment here works as dark comedy.

jokes.text: I found it in the girls' bathroom. It's so mean, Mr. Duvall.
jokes.setup: Regina brings the Burn Book to the principal — the book she herself created
jokes.punchline: 'It's so mean, Mr. Duvall.' — delivered with apparent sincerity by its own author
jokes.explanation: Regina turning herself into a victim of her own weapon is a beautiful character moment and a great irony joke. 'It's so mean' landing in the mouth of the person who wrote it is well-constructed and character-specific.

jokes.text: Is this true? Trang Pak made out with Coach Carr? / Good Lord.
jokes.setup: Mr. Duvall reads Burn Book entries
jokes.punchline: Mr. Duvall's question about Trang Pak and Coach Carr — it turns out to be true — and Ms. Norbury's 'Good Lord' implies she already knew
jokes.explanation: 'Good Lord' from Ms. Norbury is a great understated reaction — her resignation implies she's heard worse. The confirmation that Trang Pak/Coach Carr is TRUE adds a layer of dark humor.

jokes.text: What's that say? 'Kaitlyn Caussin is a...' / Fat whore.
jokes.setup: Mr. Duvall struggles to read a Burn Book entry
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury fills in the blank with 'Fat whore' in a completely flat, resigned tone
jokes.explanation: The deadpan resignation of Ms. Norbury filling in 'fat whore' as though it's an unremarkable syllable is excellent Tina Fey writing for herself. The contrast between the authority figure's flat reading and the viciousness of the words is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: At your age, you're gonna be having a lot of urges. You're gonna want to take off your clothes and touch each other. But if you do touch each other, you will get chlamydia. And die.
jokes.setup: Coach Carr is apparently giving sex ed advice to students; this is intercut with the Burn Book chaos
jokes.punchline: 'You will get chlamydia. And die.' — the exaggerated, inaccurate consequence delivered with absolute certainty is a perfect parody of fear-based abstinence education
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable moments in the film and among the best satirical jokes in this reel. 'You will get chlamydia. And die.' is a masterclass in comedic economy — the period after 'chlamydia' (the pause before 'and die') is essential. It perfectly parodies abstinence-only sex education, and the fact that Coach Carr is simultaneously being exposed in the Burn Book for inappropriate contact with a student makes it even funnier through dramatic irony. Craft and impact both very high.

jokes.text: Coach Carr. (Ms. Norbury says his name flatly after 'you will get chlamydia and die')
jokes.setup: Coach Carr has just delivered his insane sex-ed speech
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury says his name with flat, exhausted disapproval — a perfect straight-man button
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximum work. The exhausted name-call is perfect straight-man comedy — she doesn't need to say more.

jokes.text: All right, chlamydia. K-L-A...
jokes.setup: Coach Carr is interrupted by news about the Burn Book; resumes teaching after Cady is called out
jokes.punchline: He attempts to spell 'chlamydia' for the class, getting it immediately wrong ('K-L-A...') — the man who just warned about STDs can't even spell one
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic button — immediately after his authoritative warning about chlamydia, Coach Carr reveals he can't even spell it. The confidence of 'K-L-A...' (wrong from the start) is the essential ingredient. Character-specific and well-structured.

jokes.text: Miss Wieners, why would Regina refer to herself as a 'fugly slut'?
jokes.setup: Gretchen claims Regina wrote the Burn Book herself
jokes.punchline: Mr. Duvall's question is the logical response — nobody writes those things about themselves — delivered with weary administrative exasperation
jokes.explanation: Mr. Duvall's dry logical question is funny for its reasonableness — in a world of teenage hysteria, his quiet 'but why would she...' is perfect straight-man comedy. 'Fugly slut' in a school administrator's mouth adds absurdity.

jokes.text: Maybe we're not in that book because everybody likes us. And I don't wanna be punished for being well-liked. And I don't think my father, the inventor of Toaster Strudel, would be too pleased to hear about this.
jokes.setup: Gretchen and Karen defend themselves in the principal's office
jokes.punchline: 'My father, the inventor of Toaster Strudel' — the non-sequitur credential drop to intimidate the principal is completely unhinged and specific
jokes.explanation: One of the great absurdist character jokes in the film. 'The inventor of Toaster Strudel' as a shield against school discipline is so specific, so unexpected, and so perfectly Gretchen that it becomes instantly iconic. The triple setup ('maybe we're not in it because everyone likes us' + 'I don't want to be punished for being well-liked' + Toaster Strudel) escalates beautifully. Comparably exceptional to the highest-tier jokes in this reel. Originality and character integration both near-perfect.

jokes.text: Maybe we're not in that book, because everybody likes us. And I don't wanna be punished for being well-liked. And I don't think my father, the inventor of Toaster Strudel, would be too pleased to hear about this.
jokes.setup: Gretchen is in the principal's office, defending herself.
jokes.punchline: 'My father, the inventor of Toaster Strudel' — Gretchen name-dropping her dad's invention as a source of authority in a disciplinary meeting is an absurdist non sequitur that is entirely Gretchen.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Gretchen jokes in the film. 'My father, the inventor of Toaster Strudel' is both a callback to her established wealth and a perfect absurdist flex — she's invoking a breakfast pastry as a source of institutional power. The logic is entirely Gretchen: privilege means you don't get in trouble. Extremely quotable, perfectly character-integrated.

jokes.text: 'Made out with a hot dog'? Oh, my God, that was one time!
jokes.setup: Burn Book pages are being read by students in the hallway
jokes.punchline: A girl confirms that she did make out with a hot dog — 'that was one time!' — which is somehow worse than denial
jokes.explanation: The 'that was one time!' defense is a classic comedic structure — but 'made out with a hot dog' as the specific allegation is brilliantly absurd. The girl's admission-by-protest is a perfect button. Well-executed and very funny.

jokes.text: 'Dawn Schweitzer has a huge ass'? Who would write that? / Who wouldn't write that?
jokes.setup: Students are reading Burn Book entries aloud
jokes.punchline: 'Who wouldn't write that?' — the implied consensus that Dawn's ass is huge and therefore fair game is darkly funny in its casual cruelty
jokes.explanation: The reversal — 'who would write that?' / 'who wouldn't?' — is a punchy structure. Somewhat cheap (the insult itself has no craft) but the delivery works as dark comedy.

jokes.text: 'Dawn Schweitzer has a huge ass'? Who would write that? / Who wouldn't write that?
jokes.setup: Another Burn Book entry is read aloud
jokes.punchline: The question 'Who would write that?' is answered with 'Who wouldn't write that?' — implying the entry is so obvious that the question of authorship is irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy exchange with good economy. The reversal works well — 'who wouldn't write that' recontextualizes the question entirely in one beat. Slightly cheap but very efficient.

jokes.text: 'Trang Pak made out with Coach Carr'? / And so did Sun Jin Dinh.
jokes.setup: Trang Pak's entry is being read
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'and so did Sun Jin Dinh' — a second victim, delivered matter-of-factly — escalates the Coach Carr scandal
jokes.explanation: The casual addition of a second name escalates the scandal with perfect economy. The fact that someone just KNEW this information — and volunteered it immediately — implies the scandal was poorly-kept. Good callback structure.

jokes.text: Hey! Hey! Settle down! All right, hey. No. You do not push and sh...
jokes.setup: The assembly has broken into chaos with girls fighting
jokes.punchline: Duvall's increasingly futile attempts to restore order — 'You do not push and sh—' truncated by the chaos overtaking him — is a visual gag of institutional authority collapsing
jokes.explanation: Classic authority-figure-losing-control comedy. The cut-off sentence ('You do not push and sh—') is funny for what it implies. Functional escalation beat.

jokes.text: Mom, can you pick me up? I'm scared.
jokes.setup: The school is in full riot mode.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the chaos, a student calls their mom — 'I'm scared' — capturing both the absurdity of the riot and a child's authentic response to it.
jokes.explanation: Light but good. The juxtaposition of 'girls gone wild' chaos and a scared kid calling their mom is funny in its contrast. Quick and economical.

jokes.text: 'Janis Ian, dyke'? / That's original. / 'Too gay to function'?! / Hey! That's only OK when I say it.
jokes.setup: Janis and Damian read Janis's Burn Book entry
jokes.punchline: Damian objects to the Burn Book using 'too gay to function' — but his objection is that it's 'only OK when I say it,' confirming he uses it about himself
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is perfect: Damian's initial calm ('that's original' for 'dyke') followed by outrage at 'too gay to function' — but his outrage is not about the word's content but about who gets to say it. 'That's only OK when I say it' is brilliant character comedy — it subverts the expected response and reveals Damian's specific, proprietary relationship with his own identity. High craft and very quotable.

jokes.text: Yeah! Take your top off!
jokes.setup: The school is descending into chaos as the Burn Book spreads
jokes.punchline: A male student interprets the girls fighting as an opportunity to yell 'Take your top off!' — the chaos has enabled complete social breakdown
jokes.explanation: A broad escalation beat that works in context as chaos comedy but has minimal craft. It's a cheap laugh in the middle of a well-constructed chaos sequence.

jokes.text: Now, here's what we're gonna do... / Ron, come quick! They've gone wild. The girls have gone wild.
jokes.setup: School administration attempts to regain control of the chaos
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury's 'The girls have gone wild' — a riff on 'Girls Gone Wild' — delivered with bureaucratic alarm
jokes.explanation: A quick pop-culture riff that works because of Ms. Norbury's deadpan delivery. The double meaning (the actual chaos vs. the brand) is functional.

jokes.text: It was full-tilt jungle madness.
jokes.setup: Cady narrates the school-wide chaos following the Burn Book distribution
jokes.punchline: 'Full-tilt jungle madness' — Cady applying her African wildlife observer framework to American high school chaos
jokes.explanation: A callback to Cady's Africa-as-nature-documentary perspective on high school (established in earlier reels). 'Full-tilt jungle madness' is vivid, specific, and character-perfect. Good economy.

jokes.text: Hey, I pulled these two off each other. / Coach Carr, step away from the underage girls.
jokes.setup: Coach Carr tries to help restore order
jokes.punchline: Mr. Duvall immediately orders him away from the girls — implicitly referencing the Trang Pak/Sun Jin Dinh scandal
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Mr. Duvall's crisp 'step away from the underage girls' — delivered as a standard administrative order — is funny precisely because it treats the scandal as established fact that just needs to be managed. Well-constructed, economical, great character integration for Duvall as straight man.

jokes.text: Let me help you down there. / Hell, no! I did not leave the Southside for this!
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury is apparently knocked down in the chaos
jokes.punchline: 'I did not leave the Southside for this!' — Ms. Norbury's backstory as a Southside survivor is deployed as absurdist self-pity
jokes.explanation: A quick character deepening that's also funny — Ms. Norbury's Southside backstory is an unexpected detail that makes her refusal to accept help funnier. 'Hell, no!' establishes she still has that edge.

jokes.text: Oh, crap! My hair!
jokes.setup: The school chaos is escalating
jokes.punchline: In the middle of physical fighting, someone's primary concern is her hair
jokes.explanation: Stock joke — the vain girl worried about her hair in a fight is a cliché. Functions as a quick escalation beat but has minimal craft. Below average for this script.

jokes.text: Have you ever walked up to people and realized they were just talking about you? Have you ever had it happen 60 times in a row? I have.
jokes.setup: Cady is now completely exposed — everyone has seen the Burn Book, everyone knows what she did
jokes.punchline: The quantification — '60 times in a row' — escalates a relatable social anxiety into an absurdist nightmare specific to Cady's situation
jokes.explanation: A smart closing beat. The observational hook ('have you ever walked up to people and realized they were talking about you?') is universally relatable, but the '60 times in a row' escalation makes it specific to this nightmare scenario. Good structure: relatable → specific → absurd.

jokes.text: And from young ladies. I got parents calling me on the phone asking, 'Did someone get shot?'
jokes.setup: Principal Duvall is scolding students for bad behavior in a standard disciplinary speech.
jokes.punchline: The behavior was so extreme that parents assumed gun violence was involved — a wildly disproportionate escalation.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of the comedic escalation — a school girl fight being mistaken for a shooting is absurd and sharp. Duvall's delivery of bureaucratic outrage is well-characterized. It's a strong opener for the assembly scene.

jokes.text: Coach Carr has fled school property. Ms. Norbury has been accused of selling drugs.
jokes.setup: Duvall is cataloguing consequences of the Burn Book fallout in bureaucratic, matter-of-fact language.
jokes.punchline: The sheer mundane delivery of two completely absurd institutional disasters — a teacher fled and another is accused of dealing — lands as dry comedy.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Duvall's bureaucratic deadpan listing genuine catastrophes. Works especially well on rewatch because we know Coach Carr's subplot. The pairing of two disasters in rapid succession is efficient.

jokes.text: I will keep you here all night. / We can't keep them past 4. / I will keep you here until 4.
jokes.setup: Duvall builds an authoritative threat: 'I don't care how long it takes, I will keep you here all night.'
jokes.punchline: He's immediately corrected on the legal limitation, and without missing a beat, issues the deflated version of the same threat.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the reel. The structure is perfect: big authoritative declaration → quiet deflation → character doubles down on the smaller version with identical energy. It's deeply character-specific (Duvall the impotent authority figure), economical to the point of perfection, and gets a genuine laugh every time. The joke earns its 8+ because the comedic architecture is impeccable — the punchline IS the deflation itself, delivered with no editorializing.

jokes.text: Somebody wrote in that book that I'm lying about being a virgin because I use super-jumbo tampons. But I can't help it if I've got a heavy flow and a wide-set vagina.
jokes.setup: Principal Duvall asks who has a 'lady problem' they'd like to discuss, expecting something tame.
jokes.punchline: A student immediately volunteers gynecological TMI with total sincerity and zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely iconic joke. The comedy operates on multiple levels: misdirection (we expect a catty social problem, not anatomy), the character's oblivious sincerity, and the specific absurdity of 'wide-set vagina' as a phrase. High quotability — this line has genuine cultural staying power. The impact is enormous because the room laugh is partly embarrassed and partly delighted. Loses a point on character integration since the student is unnamed, but it's a brilliantly written one-shot.

jokes.text: Yeah, I can't do this.
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury has just heard the 'wide-set vagina' confession delivered with total earnestness.
jokes.punchline: Her immediate, flat resignation — 'I can't do this' — is the perfect straight-woman collapse.
jokes.explanation: A four-word reaction beat that maximizes economy. Norbury's character — the exhausted, competent adult surrounded by chaos — is perfectly expressed. The joke exists in context only but it's a great button on the previous joke.

jokes.text: It's not a self-esteem problem. I think they're all pretty pleased with themselves.
jokes.setup: Principal Duvall asks Ms. Norbury to say something to help students with their self-esteem.
jokes.punchline: Norbury subverts the premise — the girls' problem isn't low self-esteem, it's the opposite: they're arrogantly overconfident.
jokes.explanation: Smart satirical observation that inverts the after-school-special premise the film is simultaneously embodying. 'Pretty pleased with themselves' is a brilliantly dry formulation. This is Tina Fey's authorial voice coming through Norbury — the whole movie is a critique of girl-world arrogance dressed as an empowerment story.

jokes.text: There's been some girl-on-girl crime here.
jokes.setup: Everyone raises their hands admitting to gossiping about friends — a mass revelation of social betrayal.
jokes.punchline: Norbury deadpans a riff on 'friendly fire' / crime terminology to describe it, treating mean girl behavior like a legal offense.
jokes.explanation: Economical, punchy, and quotable. The reframing of social cruelty as 'crime' is a smart satirical move that's both funny and thematically pointed. The wordplay is light but effective.

jokes.text: You've been acting really stuck-up ever since you switched to shortfielder. And Dawn agrees with me. / Dawn? / Don't drag me into this, I'm pitching tomorrow.
jokes.setup: The workshop exercises begin, and we cut to various cliques having their confrontations — the jock girls are supposedly doing emotional work.
jokes.punchline: Their 'clique problem' is petty sports hierarchy drama; Dawn refuses to be involved because she has a game tomorrow — completely missing the point of emotional vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny montage beat. 'I'm pitching tomorrow' as a reason to avoid emotional confrontation is a good character-specific deflection. Not a standout but efficiently funny.

jokes.text: Can I just say that we don't have a clique problem at this school? And some of us shouldn't have to take this workshop, because some of us are just victims in this situation.
jokes.setup: The workshop is meant for everyone to take accountability.
jokes.punchline: A student immediately exempts herself by declaring herself a victim — which is itself a clique behavior and denies the entire premise of the workshop.
jokes.explanation: Solid observational comedy about how people who most need to change are always most certain they don't. Functions as setup for the follow-up punchline.

jokes.text: That's probably true. How many of you have ever felt personally victimized by Regina George?
jokes.setup: Student claims to be just a victim, not part of the problem.
jokes.punchline: Norbury casually validates her and pivots to asking the entire gymnasium if they've been victimized by one person — implying Regina's cruelty is so universal it's its own category.
jokes.explanation: The most quotable line in this reel and arguably the most iconic in the film. 'Personally victimized by Regina George' has become a cultural shorthand. The structure is flawless: validates the previous joke (That's probably true) then immediately weaponizes it. The word 'personally' does enormous work — it makes Regina sound like a one-woman crime wave. High craft because the line functions simultaneously as joke, character assassination of Regina, and plot point. Earns 8+ because it's genuinely exceptional and culturally durable.

jokes.text: Just that you sell drugs. / No.
jokes.setup: Norbury asks Cady if she ever made up a rumor about anybody, expecting her to say no.
jokes.punchline: Cady admits that the one rumor she started was about Norbury herself — the teacher asking the question.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing in the exchange. The structure is a classic trap-door: Norbury assumes the answer will be 'no,' but the answer implicates her directly. The 'No.' response is the right button — it doesn't oversell the joke. The callback to earlier events gives it added resonance for viewers.

jokes.text: 'Alyssa, I'm sorry I called you a gap-toothed bitch.' 'It's not your fault you're so gap-toothed.'
jokes.setup: Students are supposed to write sincere apology letters.
jokes.punchline: The 'apology' immediately qualifies itself into a backhanded insult — she's still calling Alyssa gap-toothed, just more politely.
jokes.explanation: Classic non-apology apology comedy. The joke structure is tight: the second sentence undoes the first completely by repeating the insult as a compassionate observation. The 'it's not your fault' construction is hilariously insincere. This is sharp writing about how performative apologies work.

jokes.text: 'Gretchen, I'm sorry I laughed at you that time you got diarrhea at Barnes and Noble.' 'And I'm sorry I told everyone about it.' And I'm sorry for repeating it now.
jokes.setup: Student reads an apology for a humiliating incident — standard cringe territory.
jokes.punchline: The apology compounds its own sin in real time by adding 'and I'm sorry for repeating it now' — which is itself another repetition.
jokes.explanation: The self-canceling apology escalates beautifully. First the specific humiliation (diarrhea at Barnes and Noble is a brilliantly mundane detail), then the meta-layer: apologizing for the apology within the apology. The joke is structurally elegant — it performs the crime it's apologizing for. Good craft.

jokes.text: Laura, I don't hate you because you're fat. You're fat because I hate you.
jokes.setup: Pattern of backhanded apology letters has been established — we expect another non-apology.
jokes.punchline: This one drops the pretense entirely and flips the logic to something genuinely vicious and oddly philosophical.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire film. The structure is devastatingly precise: 13 words, perfect symmetry, a logical reversal that is simultaneously more honest and more cruel than a standard insult. 'You're fat because I hate you' is paradoxical nonsense that somehow lands as a profound statement of mean-girl psychology — the cruelty is the cause, not the response. Near-perfect economy (10 words of real content), highly original formulation, massively quotable. Earns 8.5+ because it has the precision of a great aphorism weaponized as a joke.

jokes.text: I just wish we could all get along like we used to in middle school. I wish that I could bake a cake made out of rainbows and smiles, and we'd all eat it and be happy.
jokes.setup: In the midst of raw, cutting confessions, a workshop exercise for emotional catharsis.
jokes.punchline: An unhinged, deeply sincere non-sequitur about a cake made of rainbows and smiles — a hysterical tonal contrast from the viciousness preceding it.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the tonal whiplash — immediately following the vicious 'you're fat because I hate you' comes total emotional sincerity from a random student. The specificity of 'rainbows and smiles' as cake ingredients elevates it from generic naivety to genuinely absurdist poetry. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: She doesn't even go here!
jokes.setup: An unknown crying girl has just delivered a heartfelt rainbow cake speech to the entire school assembly.
jokes.punchline: Ms. Norbury's flat, incredulous 'she doesn't even go here' reveals the student is a total stranger who wandered in.
jokes.explanation: Iconic. Five words that do everything. The joke rewards the absurdist setup (who is this person?) by revealing the most mundane-yet-ridiculous explanation. This line has become a cultural meme used to describe anyone out of place in a situation. The comedic economy is perfect — no word is wasted. The structure is a classic delayed punchline with maximum impact. Earns high marks because it's both a great joke in context AND a free-standing quotable phrase.

jokes.text: Do you even go to this school? / No. I just have a lot of feelings. / OK, go home.
jokes.setup: Norbury confirms the girl doesn't go to the school.
jokes.punchline: 'I just have a lot of feelings' as a reason for being there, followed by the flattest possible dismissal: 'OK, go home.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect triple: the discovery (she doesn't go here), the absurd justification ('I just have a lot of feelings'), and the bureaucratic non-reaction ('OK, go home').
