Each beat escalates the joke. 'I just have a lot of feelings' is a highly quotable line that has taken on independent life. The whole sequence is a masterclass in comedic economy.

jokes.text: I'm sorry that people are so jealous of me. But I can't help it that I'm popular.
jokes.setup: Students are giving apologies in the workshop.
jokes.punchline: This student's 'apology' is entirely self-aggrandizing — she's apologizing on behalf of other people's jealousy of her popularity.
jokes.explanation: Another sharp non-apology apology, following the established pattern. Less surprising at this point in the sequence but still lands as a solid character beat — perfectly captures a certain type of oblivious narcissism.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Oh, jeez. OK, walk it off. Walk it off. / They're OK.
jokes.setup: Students are doing trust falls or some physical exercise as part of the workshop.
jokes.punchline: Someone clearly gets hurt — the panicked 'walk it off' and reassuring 'they're OK' suggest a comically bad outcome from a team-building exercise.
jokes.explanation: Inferred physical comedy from dialogue context. The humor is in the visual (trust fall gone wrong at an anti-bullying workshop) and the adults' breezy damage-control response. Functional slapstick, elevated by context but medium craft since we're inferring it from dialogue.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. It's her dream come true, diving into a big pile of girls.
jokes.setup: Ms. Norbury is managing the physical trust-fall exercises.
jokes.punchline: A student makes a lewd insinuation about Ms. Norbury's sexuality in the context of her literally catching girls.
jokes.explanation: Mean-spirited but contextually appropriate — this is exactly the kind of thing mean girls would say. It's not particularly clever but it's character-authentic. The joke exists primarily to show that the workshop isn't fixing anything yet.

jokes.text: Janis's public confession — she convinced Cady to befriend Regina to destroy her, they laughed at her, gave her weight-gain candy bars, turned her friends against her — and 'we gave you foot cream instead of face wash.'
jokes.setup: Janis takes the microphone, ostensibly to give an apology in the workshop.
jokes.punchline: Instead of apologizing, she delivers a gleeful full confession of an elaborate years-long revenge scheme, escalating with each detail — culminating in the mundane foot cream detail.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure works beautifully — each item is worse than the last, but the foot cream callback is the perfect absurdist low-stakes button after the high-stakes items. Janis's character is perfectly served: she's the one person unashamed to confess because she's proud of it. The joke of using the apology workshop as a confession platform is sharp meta-commentary.

jokes.text: God! I am so sorry, Regina. Really, I don't know why I did it. I guess it's probably because I've got a big lesbian crush on you. / Suck on that!
jokes.setup: Janis has been confessing all her schemes against Regina — the audience expects her to wrap with a sincere apology.
jokes.punchline: She claims her motivation was a 'big lesbian crush' on Regina and immediately follows with 'Suck on that!' — turning the confession into a triumphant mockery.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character payoff — Janis reclaims the lesbian rumor that was used against her and uses it to embarrass Regina instead. The 'suck on that' is perfect character voice: triumphant, adolescent, and utterly unrepentant. The joke is both funny and a character-arc moment.

jokes.text: Suck on that! / Janis! Janis! Janis! Janis!
jokes.setup: Janis has just delivered her scorched-earth non-apology.
jokes.punchline: She exits to a crowd chanting her name as if she's a sports hero, while adults scramble. The absurd triumphalism of 'Suck on that!' punctuates the chaos.
jokes.explanation: Good energy payoff to the Janis speech. The crowd chanting her name is the kind of absurd escalation that earns a big laugh in a theater. 'Suck on that' is perfectly in character — crude and triumphant.

jokes.text: They say that you're a home-schooled jungle freak, who's a less-hot version of me.
jokes.setup: Regina is furious and confronting Cady, who is pleading with her.
jokes.punchline: Regina's most cutting insult is simultaneously deeply personal to Cady and utterly self-centered — even in insulting someone else, Regina makes it about her own hotness.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Regina characterization — 'a less-hot version of me' is so narcissistically specific that it's both a devastating insult to Cady and an inadvertent self-parody of Regina. 'Home-schooled jungle freak' as an insult is sharp in its specificity. High character integration because only Regina would phrase an insult this way.

jokes.text: And that's how Regina George died. No, I'm totally kidding. But she did get hurt. Some girls say they saw her head go all the way around.
jokes.setup: Regina storms out into traffic after the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Cady's narration teases that Regina died — a fake-out — then matter-of-factly confirms she 'did get hurt' and adds the absurd detail that her head 'went all the way around.'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection with a dark subversive twist. 'That's how Regina George died' as a cold open fake-out is the most effective structure here. 'No, I'm totally kidding' is the right amount of casual about it. The 'head go all the way around' detail is excellent absurdist escalation. The follow-up about being accused of pushing her adds another layer.

jokes.text: Some people swear they saw me push her in front of the bus. That was an even worse rumor.
jokes.setup: Cady has just said the head-spinning rumor is false.
jokes.punchline: She calls being accused of pushing someone in front of a bus an 'even worse rumor' — which is dry understatement given that it's a murder accusation.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan button on the previous joke. The understatement of calling a murder accusation 'an even worse rumor' (rather than something like 'a serious legal problem') is characteristically Cady — she's still thinking in high-school social terms even about attempted murder allegations.

jokes.text: This is the fertility vase of the Ndebele tribe. Does that mean anything to you? / No.
jokes.setup: Cady's mom is upset about her vases being moved and is trying to invoke cultural significance to get through to Cady.
jokes.punchline: Cady flatly says 'No' — she has zero connection to this African tribal context, exposing the gap between her parents' world (they lived in Africa) and the American teenager she's become.
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective joke about Cady's cultural displacement. The specific tribe name (Ndebele) adds authenticity to the absurdity. 'Does that mean anything to you? No.' is a perfect one-word deflation. Works primarily as character comedy.

jokes.text: She's afraid of you. / I don't know, maybe we mainstream-schooled you too soon.
jokes.setup: Cady is upset that her mom hates her — a standard teen complaint.
jokes.punchline: Dad reframes it as the mom being 'afraid' (a funny inversion), then Mom casually wonders if they 'mainstream-schooled' her too soon — treating entering public school like a dangerous experiment.
jokes.explanation: 'Mainstream-schooled' as a verb is a sharp coinage — it frames public school as an aggressive intervention rather than a normal experience. Good character work for the earnest academic parents who treat their daughter's social life like a fieldwork experiment.

jokes.text: Remember when we saw those lions fighting over the wart hog carcass? / I'll be the wart hog.
jokes.setup: Dad is trying to prepare Cady for how bad tomorrow at school will be.
jokes.punchline: Cady predicts she'll be the wart hog carcass — the already-dead thing being fought over — which is a funny, resigned, and very specific self-deprecation from a girl raised in Africa.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever joke that works on character levels — only a girl raised in Africa would use this specific metaphor for high school social dynamics. The wart hog carcass as self-identification is both funny and unexpectedly poignant. High character integration because it could only belong to Cady.

jokes.text: You're still an excellent student, right? / Oh, yeah. I need you to sign my calculus test. / Why? / I'm failing.
jokes.setup: Dad encourages Cady to focus on her studies since at least she's still a great student.
jokes.punchline: Cady's affirmative 'Oh yeah' immediately crashes into needing a failing test signed — total contradiction of her reassurance.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed reversal. The 'Oh, yeah' false confidence makes the pivot to 'I'm failing' land harder. Good economy — the joke is told in four exchanges with no fat. The callback to her earlier self-sabotage adds meaning.

jokes.text: OK. You are... What do they call it? / Grounded. / You're grounded.
jokes.setup: Dad is about to dish out punishment for Cady's failing grade.
jokes.punchline: Dad doesn't even know the word 'grounded' — revealing how out-of-touch these academic parents are with normal American parenting — and needs Mom to supply the term.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The parents' obliviousness to standard American parenting vocabulary is perfectly observed — they're anthropologists who've never raised a kid in mainstream America. Needing your spouse to supply the word 'grounded' mid-sentence is a great beat. High character integration because this joke could only exist in the context of Cady's specific family.

jokes.text: Did your teacher ever try to sell you marijuana or Ecstasy tablets? / No. / What are marijuana tablets?
jokes.setup: School officials are interviewing students about Ms. Norbury's alleged drug dealing.
jokes.punchline: Aaron first says no, then immediately asks what marijuana tablets are — revealing the question was based on a drug that doesn't exist in that form, exposing the investigation's absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke about bureaucratic absurdity — 'marijuana tablets' is a thing that doesn't exist, suggesting whoever wrote the investigation protocol doesn't know drugs either. Aaron's earnest 'What are marijuana tablets?' is both funny and exposes the investigation as farcical. Good economy.

jokes.text: After the allegations against Coach Carr turned out to be extremely true...
jokes.setup: Duvall is explaining why the school must investigate every Burn Book claim.
jokes.punchline: 'Turned out to be extremely true' — the casual adverb 'extremely' applied to a teacher's misconduct is a brilliantly dry understatement, implying something much worse than the investigation uncovered.
jokes.explanation: 'Extremely true' as a modifier for a scandal is a great Fey construction — the word 'extremely' does comic work by implying degrees of truth exist, and by suggesting the situation was more lurid than disclosed. Classic deadpan understatement.

jokes.text: That book was written by a bunch of stupid girls who make up rumors because they're bored with their own lame lives.
jokes.setup: Aaron is defending Ms. Norbury against the drug allegations.
jokes.punchline: He delivers what sounds like a righteous defense but is simultaneously an accurate — and funny — description of the girls he's been hanging out with, including his ex-girlfriend.
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — Aaron doesn't realize he's describing Cady and her crew. Competent but not particularly original or sharp. The joke depends on dramatic irony the audience has but Aaron doesn't, which is a bit easy.

jokes.text: Oh, hi. Did you wanna buy some drugs? / I'm just done with my quiz. / Wait. I'll grade it right now.
jokes.setup: Cady narrates that Ms. Norbury is 'living proof that no good deed goes unpunished' — she's being investigated for drug dealing despite being a good teacher.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Norbury sarcastically greeting a student with 'Did you wanna buy some drugs?' — she's so over the investigation she's making jokes about it herself.
jokes.explanation: A great character-specific joke — Norbury's coping mechanism is sarcasm, and greeting a student with 'did you wanna buy some drugs' perfectly expresses her exhausted cynicism about the whole situation. The pivot to 'I'll grade it right now' shows she's still a dedicated teacher even while making drug jokes. High character integration.

jokes.text: I gotta say, watching the police search my house really was the cherry on top of a fantastic year.
jokes.setup: Cady is narrating the consequences of her confession.
jokes.punchline: 'The cherry on top of a fantastic year' as a description of police searching her home — maximally ironic understatement.
jokes.explanation: Standard ironic understatement — 'cherry on top of a fantastic year' for a police raid is reliable but not particularly innovative. Gets the job done as narration but doesn't stand out in a dense script.

jokes.text: That's all right. Getting hit by a bus is pretty good punishment.
jokes.setup: Cady explains she didn't name Gretchen and Karen as co-authors of the Burn Book because she's trying not to talk about people behind their backs.
jokes.punchline: Norbury casually responds that getting hit by a bus is 'pretty good punishment' anyway — a darkly comic acceptance of karma-by-vehicle.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Norbury — her dark, dry humor about Regina's bus injury is both funny and slightly cathartic. 'Pretty good punishment' as a clinical assessment of a traumatic accident is excellent deadpan.

jokes.text: Welcome back, nerd.
jokes.setup: Cady scores 94 on the makeup math test after Norbury has been grading her work.
jokes.punchline: Norbury's dry 'Welcome back, nerd' — an affectionate but blunt acknowledgment that Cady's intelligence was always there, just buried under social ambition.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do a lot of work. 'Welcome back, nerd' is both funny and genuinely warm — it's Norbury's way of saying Cady has returned to herself. The economy is near-perfect. The joke is small but precisely right.

jokes.text: Marymount, you sons of bitches. You no-good sons of bitches.
jokes.setup: The Mathletes are about to compete at the state championship — a high-pressure but inherently nerdy context.
jokes.punchline: Kevin delivers a pre-game trash-talk speech more appropriate for a football game — treating a math competition with hyper-masculine sports bravado.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from tonal collision — the intensity of sports-movie trash talk applied to a math competition is delightfully absurd. Kevin's character (the Mathlete who raps, who has intense sports energy for academic contests) is perfectly served. 'You no-good sons of bitches' as a repeated beat escalates effectively.

jokes.text: Don't be. You can do this. There's nothing to break your focus, because not one of those Marymount boys is cute.
jokes.setup: Kevin is trying to motivate Cady before the math competition.
jokes.punchline: His motivational speech pivots to 'not one of those Marymount boys is cute' — an oddly specific, slightly catty piece of competitive intel that reveals Kevin knows exactly what distracts Cady.
jokes.explanation: Kevin is funny here because he's a nerd who's also very perceptive about teenage girl psychology. 'Not one of those Marymount boys is cute' as a focus strategy is both a good joke and characterization. The specificity makes it land.

jokes.text: Where's Cady? / She went out. / She's grounded. / Are they not allowed out when they're grounded?
jokes.setup: Cady is missing from the math competition; the team is about to compete without their best player.
jokes.punchline: Kevin asks 'Are they not allowed out when they're grounded?' — exposing that he genuinely doesn't understand what grounding is, in a parallel to Cady's own parents.
jokes.explanation: A quiet callback — another character who doesn't understand normal American parenting conventions, which is funny given Cady's own parents' confusion. It suggests the whole world around Cady is populated by people slightly outside mainstream teenage experience.

jokes.text: Don't forget to vote for Spring Fling King and Queen, people. These A-holes will represent you for a full calendar year.
jokes.setup: Standard school-dance-pep announcement about voting for prom royalty.
jokes.punchline: 'These A-holes will represent you for a full calendar year' — an MC who can't be bothered to pretend the tradition is meaningful.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical commentary on school popularity contests delivered through an MC who's clearly over it. 'These A-holes' is surprisingly strong language for a school dance and that's part of the joke. The 'full calendar year' specificity adds to the absurdity — as if representing for less time would be acceptable.

jokes.text: I'm gonna vote for Regina George because she got hit by that bus. / I'm voting for Cady Heron because she pushed her.
jokes.setup: Students are deciding who to vote for Spring Fling Queen.
jokes.punchline: Both votes are based on bus-related violence — one for being a victim, one for being the alleged perpetrator. Trauma has become a popularity qualifier.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke — the two students mirror each other's reasoning but from opposite sides of the incident, arriving at the same voting conclusion. The dark absurdity that bus violence has become a democratic credential is very sharp satire. Well constructed.

jokes.text: Miss Caroline Krafft seriously needed to pluck her eyebrows. Her outfit looked like it was picked out by a blind Sunday school teacher. And she had some 99-cent lip gloss on her snaggletooth.
jokes.setup: Cady is facing her math opponent Caroline Krafft in the sudden-death round, under enormous pressure.
jokes.punchline: Cady's inner monologue immediately reverts to catty mean-girl observations about Caroline's appearance — she's been conditioned to process threats through personal appearance critique.
jokes.explanation: 'Picked out by a blind Sunday school teacher' is an exquisitely specific insult — it's both vivid and hilarious. The function of this joke is thematic (Cady's mean-girl conditioning runs deep) and the execution is sharp. 'Snaggletooth' with 99-cent lip gloss is a great comedic detail. The monologue exists to set up the subsequent moral epiphany, which makes it structurally earned.

jokes.text: Calling somebody else fat won't make you any skinnier. Calling someone stupid doesn't make you any smarter. And ruining Regina George's life definitely didn't make me any happier.
jokes.setup: Cady has just catalogued Caroline Krafft's flaws — a reflex mean-girl response.
jokes.punchline: She pivots to a genuine moral epiphany that's also slightly funny in its three-part structure — especially the third term, which escalates from generic wisdom to the specific absurdity of her own life.
jokes.explanation: More thematic than purely comedic, but the three-part structure — with 'ruining Regina George's life' as the escalating specific third term — is a Fey hallmark. The joke is in the contrast between the universal wisdom of the first two and the hyper-specific absurdity of the third. Quotable.

jokes.text: The limit is negative one. / Oh, crap. I lost.
jokes.setup: In sudden death, Caroline answers first — Cady is processing whether Caroline got it right.
jokes.punchline: Caroline confidently says 'negative one,' and Cady immediately concludes she's lost — which turns out to be wrong (it's incorrect), but the reflexive defeat is funny.
jokes.explanation: A quick beat. 'Oh, crap. I lost.' as a resigned inner reaction that turns out to be premature is functional but not particularly crafted. Gets a mild laugh from the wrong assumption.

jokes.text: Limits. That was the week Aaron got his hair cut. Oh, God, he looked so cute. OK, focus, Cady.
jokes.setup: Cady needs to remember what she learned about limits in math. She tries to use memory association.
jokes.punchline: Her memory association leads her directly to Aaron's haircut, then she has to tell herself to focus — she's remembering calculus through the lens of her crush.
jokes.explanation: A charming and very character-specific joke — Cady's memory palace for calculus is organized by her crush's haircuts. The self-correcting 'OK, focus, Cady' makes it funnier because it shows she's genuinely struggling against her own teenage brain. Good character integration.

jokes.text: The limit does not exist. / The limit does not exist!
jokes.setup: Cady has been asked to solve the limits problem; she arrives at her answer after a moment of genuine revelation.
jokes.punchline: She says 'The limit does not exist' quietly, then immediately repeats it louder — the double delivery is funny because it mirrors the moment an answer crystallizes from uncertainty to conviction.
jokes.explanation: The phrase has become deeply quotable far beyond its mathematical context — 'the limit does not exist' has taken on a life as a general expression of ambition/boundary-pushing. In context it's a satisfying payoff after Cady's internal struggle. The double delivery builds the moment. High quotability score reflects its cultural afterlife.

jokes.text: How do you like me now? You like that? Yeah! Get some! Get some!
jokes.setup: North Shore wins the state math championship.
jokes.punchline: Kevin celebrates with the intensity and vocabulary of a victorious football player — again treating math competition like contact sport.
jokes.explanation: Consistent character comedy — Kevin's hyper-athletic energy applied to math. The joke pays off his opening trash talk. 'Get some! Get some!' at a math championship is delightful absurdism. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Africa, you did the damn thing. / Thanks, K.G.
jokes.setup: Kevin is congratulating Cady on winning the math competition.
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'Africa' as a nickname (referencing her upbringing) — and Cady responds 'Thanks, K.G.' with equal casual familiarity, suggesting they've bonded.
jokes.explanation: A quick, warm joke. 'Africa' as a nickname is funny because it's based entirely on where she grew up rather than any personality trait. The mutual nickname exchange signals genuine friendship formed through Mathletes. Efficient character moment.

jokes.text: We're gonna look so kick-ass in these when we roll into Spring Fling. / Oh, no, I'm not going. / What? / Cady, this is your night. Don't let the haters stop you from doing your thang. / Did you just say 'thang'?
jokes.setup: Kevin is excited about wearing their championship jackets to Spring Fling.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's motivational speech ends with 'doing your thang' — and Cady, who's been impressed by his pep talk, can't let 'thang' pass unchallenged. The vocabulary slips the mask.
jokes.explanation: 'Did you just say thang?' punctures Kevin's motivational speech perfectly. The joke is that Kevin code-switches into inspirational-speak and accidentally reveals the seam. Good beat.

jokes.text: And I could not be happier that this school year's ending.
jokes.setup: Duvall is giving a standard Spring Fling pep speech about nominees being winners.
jokes.punchline: He editorializes that he 'could not be happier' the year is over — dropping all pretense of administrative enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Duvall, who has been exhausted and beleaguered all film. Dropping the professional mask at the Spring Fling is a satisfying callback to his character's arc. The understatement is well-timed.

jokes.text: The winner of the Spring Fling Queen, future co-chair of the Student Activities Board and winner of two gift certificates to the Walker Brothers Pancake House, Cady Heron.
jokes.setup: Duvall announces the Spring Fling Queen in a formal ceremony.
jokes.punchline: The royal title is 'future co-chair of the Student Activities Board' and 'winner of two gift certificates to the Walker Brothers Pancake House' — the most anticlimactic royal honors imaginable.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of royalty into pancake gift certificates is perfectly absurd. 'Walker Brothers Pancake House' is specific enough to be funny on its own. The joke satirizes how small and local these big teen status moments actually are.

jokes.text: Half the people in this room are mad at me. And the other half only like me because they think I pushed somebody in front of a bus. So that's not good.
jokes.setup: Cady has just been crowned Spring Fling Queen and is giving an acceptance speech.
jokes.punchline: 'So that's not good' as the button after a candid audit of her social situation — the understatement is funny because the situation is objectively terrible.
jokes.explanation: A great speech moment. The structure is clean: two parallel observations → deadpan understatement button. 'That's not good' as the conclusion of a social catastrophe audit is perfect Cady voice — she's matter-of-fact about chaos. The fact that half the room likes her for a potential felony is the dark joke. High impact because it gets a room laugh AND is a character-defining moment.

jokes.text: I mean, it's just plastic. Could really just... Share it. A piece for Gretchen Wieners, a partial Spring Fling Queen.
jokes.setup: Cady is pondering the tiara — why do people stress over this thing?
jokes.punchline: She literally breaks the crown and starts distributing pieces — Duvall dryly notes 'seriously, most people just take the crown and go' — the absurdist gesture of democratizing a plastic tiara by shattering it.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of breaking a crown and distributing shards is a great visual joke, and 'a partial Spring Fling Queen' as an official title for Gretchen is funny. Duvall's aside ('most people just take the crown and go') is a perfect dry button. Good character integration — only Cady, who was never indoctrinated into the symbolism of the crown, would do this.

jokes.text: Seriously, most people just take the crown and go.
jokes.setup: Cady is breaking the tiara and handing out pieces at the microphone.
jokes.punchline: Duvall's aside — exhausted, matter-of-fact — that most queens just take the crown and leave, implying this is the most unusual behavior he's seen even in an already unusual year.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the crown-breaking joke. Duvall's one job tonight is to crown a queen, and even that has gone wrong. The economy is excellent — nine words that express a year's worth of Duvall's exhaustion.

jokes.text: And a piece for Regina George. She fractured her spine, and she still looks like a rock star.
jokes.setup: Cady is distributing tiara pieces and getting to Regina.
jokes.punchline: 'She fractured her spine, and she still looks like a rock star' — a compliment that casually acknowledges the spine fracture as if it's a minor inconvenience, with the backhanded implication that of course Regina would look good even injured.
jokes.explanation: The dark humor here is in the casual bracketing of a spinal fracture — 'she fractured her spine, and she still looks like a rock star' treats severe injury as a parenthetical. It's also slightly character-subversive: Cady is genuinely complimenting Regina, which is a growth moment, but Fey still makes it funny.

jokes.text: God, Mr. Duvall, can you wrap it up?
jokes.setup: Duvall has taken the microphone back to close out the crown ceremony.
jokes.punchline: A student in the crowd heckles the principal to hurry up — total inversion of authority at a school event.
jokes.explanation: Quick comic beat — the authority figure being heckled at the authority-figure event is a reliable but mild joke. Functional, not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Look. I'm a queen. / As am I.
jokes.setup: The tiara pieces have been distributed, and Cady's outsider friends also got pieces.
jokes.punchline: Janis declares herself a queen with mock-regality; Damian matches her with 'As am I' — an over-formal phrasing that plays on Damian being gay and both of them being gleefully outside the system.
jokes.explanation: 'As am I' is funny because of its formality — it's the phrasing of someone who has been waiting their whole life to claim this title. High character integration: Damian's gay flamboyance and Janis's outsider status make this the perfect moment for both of them.

jokes.text: So are we still in a fight? / Are you still an asshole? / I don't think so. / Well, then I guess we're OK.
jokes.setup: Aaron approaches Cady after the crown ceremony — they've been fighting.
jokes.punchline: His 'Are you still an asshole?' as a reconciliation condition is shockingly direct and funny, followed by Cady's 'I don't think so' — a hilariously uncertain answer to whether she's reformed.
jokes.explanation: 'Are you still an asshole?' as the terms of reconciliation is both funny and characteristically blunt. 'I don't think so' is the perfect answer — confident enough to be funny, uncertain enough to be honest. The exchange is sharp and efficient.

jokes.text: I was so nervous. They made us do limits. I thought I was gonna hurl. / How's your stomach now? / It's fine. / Do you feel nauseous at all? / No. / Have you been drinking? / No. / OK. / Grool.
jokes.setup: Aaron and Cady are reconnecting; he's asking about her state at the math competition.
jokes.punchline: His series of increasingly clinical questions ('Have you been drinking?') culminates in Cady's attempt at a word — 'Grool' — which is a portmanteau of 'great' and 'cool' that isn't a real word, delivered as if it's normal.
jokes.explanation: 'Grool' is a genuinely inspired coinage — a nervous portmanteau that reveals Cady is so flustered around Aaron that she can't form words correctly. The buildup of Aaron's medical-intake questions makes the final 'OK' a satisfying pause before the punchline. High originality: accidental word-merge as a character moment is both specific to Cady and highly quotable. The joke earns 8+ because the coinage is memorable, the character integration is perfect, and the buildup is well-structured.

jokes.text: You Puerto Rican? / Lebanese. / I feel that.
jokes.setup: A guy at Spring Fling approaches Janis.
jokes.punchline: 'I feel that' as a response to being told someone is Lebanese — a completely non-sequitur expression of solidarity that makes no sense but is delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke — three lines, one laugh. The comic gap between 'Lebanese' and 'I feel that' as a response is perfect. 'I feel that' implies cultural understanding where there is none, which is both absurd and very true to adolescent male social posturing.

jokes.text: Regina's spine healed, and her physical therapist taught her to channel all her rage into sports. It was perfect because the jock girls weren't afraid of her.
jokes.setup: Narration wraps up what happened to Regina after the bus incident.
jokes.punchline: Regina's sociopathic rage, which terrorized a school, is neatly redirected into sports — where it's apparently a feature, not a bug. The 'jock girls weren't afraid of her' implies everyone else still was.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical observation — the jock girls being unafraid of Regina while presumably everyone else still is implies nothing has actually changed about Regina, just the arena. The physical therapist 'teaching her to channel rage' is funny clinical language for a genuinely scary person.

jokes.text: Karen used her special talents to do the morning weather announcements. / Hi. This is Karen Smith. It's 68 degrees, and there's a 30 percent chance that it's already raining.
jokes.setup: Narration explains Karen found her calling.
jokes.punchline: 'There's a 30 percent chance that it's already raining' — a weather forecast that hedges on current conditions that are observable right now, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire film. 'A 30 percent chance that it's already raining' is an absurdist masterpiece — it's forecasting something you could verify by looking out a window, implying Karen doesn't understand the basic premise of meteorology. The joke is perfectly calibrated to Karen's specific brand of confidence-meets-obliviousness. Maximum economy: one sentence that tells you everything about Karen's mind. Earns 8.5+ because the concept is genuinely original, the character integration is flawless, and the punchline is structurally perfect.

jokes.text: And Gretchen found herself a new clique and a new queen bee to serve.
jokes.setup: Narration describes Gretchen's fate after the Plastics dissolved.
jokes.punchline: Gretchen hasn't grown or changed — she's just found a new queen to be subordinate to. The visual of her in a new clique doing the same thing implies her personality is entirely defined by servitude.
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective satirical note — Gretchen's arc is that she has no arc. The joke is in the lack of growth, which is both funny and kind of sad. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Hey, check it out. Junior Plastics.
jokes.setup: Cady narrates that Girl World is finally at peace.
jokes.punchline: Damian spots a new generation of mean girls — 'Junior Plastics' — immediately after the peace declaration, suggesting the cycle is unbreakable.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke — the film's resolution is immediately undercut by the revelation that The Plastics regenerate. 'Junior Plastics' as a taxonomic term (like a minor league) is sharp. The economy is excellent: two words that do enormous thematic work.

jokes.text: And if any freshmen tried to disturb that peace... Well, let's just say we knew how to take care of it. / [Bus sound effect or visual of bus] / Just kidding.
jokes.setup: Cady implies they 'knew how to take care of' problems.
jokes.punchline: 'Just kidding' — implying she was threatening to push freshmen in front of a bus, which she's now disavowing.
jokes.explanation: A perfect dark-comedy button for the entire film. The 'Well, let's just say we knew how to take care of it' is an ominous mob-movie construction, made funny because we know exactly what 'taking care of it' means in this movie's context. 'Just kidding' is the right deflation — it acknowledges the joke without overexplaining it. A great closing note that wraps the film's dark-comedy engine with a bow.
